# Exponential Smoothing

## Data statement

All data in this section are public data sets that come with R packages (`marathon`, `oil`, `books` and `uschange` from `fpp2`, and `Nile` and `co2` from base R) or are simulated. None of them contain personal information, so no consent, anonymisation or POPIA steps were needed.

### Overview of the methods

Exponential smoothing forecasts are weighted averages of past observations, with weights that decrease exponentially the further back we go. Each method in @tbl-es-methods adds a component, and each component has its own smoothing parameter.

| Method                      | Components                                           | Forecast $\hat{y}_{T+h \mid T}$       | Use when                                  |
|-----------------|----------------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Simple (SES)                | level $\ell_t$ ($\alpha$)                            | $\ell_T$                              | no trend, no seasonality                  |
| Holt's linear               | level, trend $b_t$ ($\alpha, \beta$)                 | $\ell_T + hb_T$                       | a linear trend                            |
| Damped trend                | level, damped trend ($\alpha, \beta, \phi$)          | $\ell_T + (\phi + \dots + \phi^h)b_T$ | a trend that is expected to flatten out   |
| Holt-Winters additive       | level, trend, season $s_t$ ($\alpha, \beta, \gamma$) | $\ell_T + hb_T + s_{T+h-m(k+1)}$      | seasonal swings of constant size          |
| Holt-Winters multiplicative | level, trend, season ($\alpha, \beta, \gamma$)       | $(\ell_T + hb_T)s_{T+h-m(k+1)}$       | seasonal swings proportional to the level |

: Exponential smoothing methods. $m$ is the seasonal period and $k = \lfloor (h-1)/m \rfloor$. {#tbl-es-methods}

Written in error-correction form, each method becomes a state-space model with a single source of error (the ETS models). This gives a likelihood (so parameters can be estimated by maximum likelihood and models compared by AICc) and prediction intervals. `ets()` chooses between the error, trend and seasonal types automatically. In [Project 1](../projects/project-01.qmd) I implemented additive Holt-Winters with a damped trend from first principles on Eskom electricity demand.

### Simple exponential smoothing

Simple exponential smoothing (SES) forecasts the next observation with a weighted average of past observations, where the weights decrease exponentially:

$$
\hat{y}_{t+1 \mid t} = \alpha y_t + \alpha(1-\alpha) y_{t-1} + \alpha(1-\alpha)^2 y_{t-2} + \cdots, \quad 0 < \alpha < 1.
$$

The same forecast can be written as two updating equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Forecast:} \quad \hat{y}_{t+h \mid t} &= \ell_t \\
\text{Smoothing:} \quad \ell_t &= \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)\ell_{t-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

::: callout-note
## Note

The level $\ell_t$ is a local mean. Forecasts from SES are flat: there is no new information after time $T$, so every forecast is $\ell_T$.
:::

To start the recursion we need $\ell_0$, and in most cases we also need to estimate $\alpha$. Both are found by minimising the sum of squared one-step-ahead errors:

$$
\text{SSE} = \sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t - \hat{y}_{t \mid t-1})^2.
$$

## Question 1: Boston marathon

The `marathon` data are the winning times (in minutes) of the Boston marathon from 1897 to 2016.

```{r}
# Read in data:
data(marathon)
# View(marathon)

cat("Start:", start(marathon), " End:", end(marathon), " Frequency:", frequency(marathon), "\n")
```

### Writing SES from first principles

```{r}
y = marathon

# Function to implement simple exponential smoothing:
# y:      time series 
# alpha:  smoothing parameter 
# level0: initial level 
ses_fxn = function(y, alpha, level0) {
  n = length(y) 
  y_hat = numeric(n) # store estimates
  level = numeric(n) # store levels
  l = level0
  
  for (t in 1:n) {
    y_hat[t] = l 
    l        = alpha*y[t] + (1-alpha)*l
    level[t] = l
  }
  
  res = y - y_hat
  sse = sum(res^2)
  list(
    yhat      = y_hat,
    level     = level,
    residuals = res,
    sse       = sse,
    forecast  = l
  )
}

# Function to return the one-step-ahead forecast: 
ses_forecast_fxn = function(y, alpha, level0) {
  ses_fxn(y ,alpha, level0)$forecast
}

# Function to optimise:
my_sse = function(par, y) {
  ses_fxn(y, alpha = par[1], level0 = par[2])$sse
}

# Optimise:
opt = optim(par = c(0.5,y[1]), 
            fn = my_sse, 
            y = y, 
            method = 'L-BFGS-B',
            lower = c(0.0001,-Inf), 
            upper = c(0.9999, Inf))

alpha_hat = opt$par[1]
l0_hat    = opt$par[2]

my_fit = ses_fxn(y,alpha=alpha_hat,level0=l0_hat)
# my_fit$forecast

# Compare with ses():
fit = ses(y,h=1)
# fit$model$par
# fit$mean

rbind(
  mine = c(alpha = alpha_hat, l0 = l0_hat,
           sse = opt$value, forecast = my_fit$forecast),
  ses  = c(fit$model$par["alpha"], fit$model$par["l"],
           sum(residuals(fit)^2), fit$mean[1])
)
```

```{r}
# Plug ses()'s parameters into my function:
check = ses_fxn(y, alpha  = fit$model$par["alpha"],
                   level0 = fit$model$par["l"])
round(unname(check$forecast) - fit$mean[1], 10)
```

Using the `ses()` parameter estimates in my own function yields the same forecast. My estimates are very close to the `ses()` estimates ($\hat{\alpha} = `r round(alpha_hat, 4)`$ vs `r round(fit$model$par["alpha"], 4)`). The small difference is due to how each optimisation works. `ses()` maximises a likelihood rather than minimising the SSE directly.

### Point forecast and prediction interval for 2017

```{r}
n      = length(y)
z      = qnorm(0.975)
s      = sqrt(check$sse/(n-2)) 
fit95  = ses(y, h = 1, level = 95)

round(rbind(
  mine = c(forecast = unname(check$forecast),
           lower = unname(check$forecast) - z*s,
           upper = unname(check$forecast) + z*s),
  ses  = c(fit95$mean[1], fit95$lower[1], fit95$upper[1])
), 4)
```

Both give the same point forecast and 95% interval: $\hat{y}_{T+1|T} \pm 1.96\,\hat{\sigma}$, with $\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{SSE/(n-2)}$.

### Plot with fitted values

```{r}
#| label: fig-marathon
#| fig-cap: "Boston marathon winning times (grey) with the SES fitted values (one-step-ahead forecasts, pink)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

mar_plot_df = data.frame(
  year = as.numeric(time(marathon)),
  observed = as.numeric(marathon),
  fitted = as.numeric(fitted(fit))
)

ggplot(data = mar_plot_df, mapping = aes(x = year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = observed, colour = "Observed")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted, colour = "Fitted")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = "grey40", "Fitted" = "deeppink")) +
  labs(
    title = "Boston marathon winning times (1897–2016).",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Winning time (minutes)",
    colour = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

@fig-marathon shows that the fitted values follow the observations but lag one step behind them. SES has no trend term, so during the long downward trend (until about 1980) the fitted values almost always predicted a longer winning time than what is actually observed.

### Estimate of $\sigma$

```{r}
c(mine = sqrt(check$sse / (n - 2)), ses = sqrt(fit$model$sigma2))
```

A typical one-step-ahead forecast is off by about $\hat{\sigma} \approx `r round(sqrt(fit[["model"]][["sigma2"]]), 2)`$ minutes. `ses()` divides the SSE by $T-2$ to correct for the two estimated parameters.

## Question 2: Saudi Arabian oil production

```{r}
# Read in data:
data(oil)
# View(oil)

# Fit SES and forecast four years ahead:
oil_fit = ses(oil, h = 4)
oil_fit$model$par
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-oil
#| fig-cap: "Annual oil production in Saudi Arabia with SES fitted values and four-year forecasts (80% and 95% prediction intervals)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

autoplot(oil_fit) +
  autolayer(fitted(oil_fit), series = "Fitted") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Fitted" = "deeppink")) +
  labs(
    title = "Saudi Arabian oil production with SES forecasts.",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Oil (millions of tonnes)",
    colour = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

An $\hat{\alpha} \approx `r round(oil_fit[["model"]][["par"]]["alpha"], 3)`$ value means the forecast relies mostly on the last observation. The four forecasts are all equal to `r round(oil_fit$mean[1], 1)`. In @fig-oil the prediction intervals widen with the horizon.

### Prediction interval with $\hat{y} \pm 1.96s$

```{r}
# Standard deviation of the residuals:
sd_oil = sd(residuals(oil_fit))

# Manual 95% prediction interval for first forecast:
PI_oil_upper = oil_fit$mean[1] + 1.96*sd_oil
PI_oil_lower = oil_fit$mean[1] - 1.96*sd_oil

# 95% prediction interval by R:
PI_oil_R = c(oil_fit$lower[1, "95%"], oil_fit$upper[1, "95%"])

kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("$\\hat{y} \\pm 1.96\\,s$", "ses()"),
  Lower  = c(PI_oil_lower, PI_oil_R[1]),
  Upper  = c(PI_oil_upper, PI_oil_R[2]),
  SD = c(paste0("$s$ = ", round(sd_oil, 2)),
         paste0("$\\hat{\\sigma}$ = ", round(sqrt(oil_fit$model$sigma2), 2)))
), digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
col.names = c("Method", "Lower", "Upper", "SD used"))
```

The two intervals are similar but not identical. This is because they use different estimates of the standard deviation. `sd()` divides by $T-1$ (1 degree of freedom for the estimated mean) and subtracts the mean of the residuals. R uses $\hat{\sigma}^2 = \sum e_t^2/(T-2)$, which does not subtract the mean and divides by $T-2$ (2 degrees of freedom for the estimated $\alpha$ and $\ell_0$).

For $h > 1$ we cannot just use $s$, since the forecast variance grows with the horizon. For SES (the ETS(A,N,N) model) the $h$-step forecast variance is $\sigma^2[1 + \alpha^2(h-1)]$.

```{r}
h = 1:4
alpha_oil = oil_fit$model$par["alpha"]

# Forecast variance for h = 1, ..., 4:
var_h = oil_fit$model$sigma2 * (1 + alpha_oil^2 * (h - 1))
upper_manual = oil_fit$mean + qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(var_h)

kable(data.frame(h = h,
                 Upper_manual = as.numeric(upper_manual),
                 Upper_R = as.numeric(oil_fit$upper[, "95%"])),
      digits = 3,
      col.names = c("h","Upper manual", "Upper R"))
```

The formula gives exactly the same upper limits as R. In the state-space form, $\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha e_t$, so each future innovation enters the level with weight $\alpha$ and persists in all later levels. Writing $y_{T+h} = \ell_T + \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{h-1} e_{T+j} + e_{T+h}$, with independent errors $e_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$, gives $\text{Var}(y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}) = \sigma^2[1 + \alpha^2(h-1)]$, which increases linearly in $h$.

## Question 3: optim() on oil 1996--2013

```{r}
oil_sub = window(oil, start = 1996, end = 2013)
opt_oil = optim(c(0.5, oil_sub[1]), 
                my_sse, 
                y = oil_sub, 
                method = "L-BFGS-B",
                lower = c(1e-4, -Inf), 
                upper = c(0.9999, Inf))

round(rbind(
  optim = setNames(opt_oil$par, c("alpha", "l")),
  ses   = ses(oil_sub)$model$par[c("alpha", "l")]
), 4)
```

## Question 4: Paperback and hardcover book sales

### a) SES

```{r}
#| label: fig-books
#| fig-cap: "Daily sales of paperback and hardcover books over 30 days."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Read in data:
data(books)
# View(books)

books_df = data.frame(
  day = rep(1:30, times = 2),
  sales = c(books[, "Paperback"], books[, "Hardcover"]),
  type = rep(c("Paperback", "Hardcover"), each = 30)
)

ggplot(data = books_df, mapping = aes(x = day, y = sales)) +
  geom_line(col = "deeppink") +
  geom_point(col = "deeppink") +
  facet_wrap(~type, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily book sales.",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Sales"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

@fig-books shows that both series are very noisy from day to day and both have an upwards trend over the month. There is no clear seasonal pattern and 30 days of data is insufficient to estimate one reliably. The upwards trend suggests that a flat forecast (SES) will be inadequate.

```{r}
# SES:
ses_pb = ses(books[, "Paperback"], h = 4)
ses_hc = ses(books[, "Hardcover"], h = 4)

# Holt's linear method:
holt_pb = holt(books[, "Paperback"], h = 4)
holt_hc = holt(books[, "Hardcover"], h = 4)

# Training RMSE:
rmse = function(fc) {
  accuracy(fc)["Training set", "RMSE"]
} 

rmse_df = data.frame(
  Series = c("Paperback", "Hardcover"),
  SES = c(rmse(ses_pb), rmse(ses_hc)),
  Holt = c(rmse(holt_pb), rmse(holt_hc))
)
kable(rmse_df, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-books-fc
#| fig-cap: "Four-day forecasts for book sales from SES and Holt's method."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Paperback"
#|   - "Hardcover"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

autoplot(books[, "Paperback"]) +
  autolayer(ses_pb, series = "SES", PI = FALSE) +
  autolayer(holt_pb, series = "Holt", PI = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("SES" = "deeppink", "Holt" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(title = "Paperback.", x = "Day", y = "Sales", colour = "") +
  theme_minimal()

autoplot(books[, "Hardcover"]) +
  autolayer(ses_hc, series = "SES", PI = FALSE) +
  autolayer(holt_hc, series = "Holt", PI = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("SES" = "deeppink", "Holt" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(title = "Hardcover.", x = "Day", y = "Sales", colour = "") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### b) Holt's linear method

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{y}_{t+h \mid t} &= \ell_t + h b_t \\
\ell_t &= \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1}) \\
b_t &= \beta^*(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta^*) b_{t-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Holt's method has a lower training RMSE than SES for both paperback and hardcover sales (paperback: `r round(rmse(holt_pb), 2)` vs `r round(rmse(ses_pb), 2)`; hardcover: `r round(rmse(holt_hc), 2)` vs `r round(rmse(ses_hc), 2)`). However, Holt's linear method estimates two more parameters than SES, so it should always fit the training data at least as well. Training RMSE does not tell us how well a model will perform out-of-sample. Although SES is just an updating rule, `ses()` and `holt()` fit the corresponding state-space models (ETS(A,N,N) and ETS(A,A,N)) with normal errors, so both have a likelihood. This means the models can be compared using AICc, which penalises the additional parameters and is more informative about which model to choose.

```{r}
# AICc:
kable(data.frame(
  Series = c("Paperback", "Hardcover"),
  AIC_SES = c(ses_pb$model$aicc, ses_hc$model$aicc),
  AIC_Holt = c(holt_pb$model$aicc, holt_hc$model$aicc)
), digits = 1, 
row.names = FALSE, 
col.names = c("Series", "SES", "Holt"))
```

### c) Which forecasts are best?

Both series have an upward trend, but the AICc gives different answers for the two. For hardcover sales, Holt's method has a clearly lower AICc than SES (`r round(holt_hc$model$aicc, 1)` vs `r round(ses_hc$model$aicc, 1)`), even after the penalty for its two extra parameters. The trend is strong enough that SES's fitted values lag behind it, so its one-step-ahead errors are larger. For paperback sales, SES has a slightly lower AICc (`r round(ses_pb$model$aicc, 1)` vs `r round(holt_pb$model$aicc, 1)`). The paperback series is noisier, so the small improvement in fit from accounting for the trend in the data is not worth the two extra parameters. However, since the difference in AICc is less than 1, there is no real evidence that one method is better than the other for paperback sales. Overall, Holt's method is preferred for the hardcover series and SES for paperback sales but with only 30 days of data it is not reliable for long-term forecasting.

### d) Prediction intervals from the RMSE

```{r}
# Training RMSE for each fit:
rmse_ses_pb  = rmse(ses_pb)
rmse_holt_pb = rmse(holt_pb)
rmse_ses_hc  = rmse(ses_hc)
rmse_holt_hc = rmse(holt_hc)

# 95% interval using RMSE:
lower_rmse = c(ses_pb$mean[1]-1.96*rmse_ses_pb,
               holt_pb$mean[1]-1.96*rmse_holt_pb,
               ses_hc$mean[1]-1.96*rmse_ses_hc,
               holt_hc$mean[1]-1.96*rmse_holt_hc)

upper_rmse = c(ses_pb$mean[1]+1.96*rmse_ses_pb,
               holt_pb$mean[1]+1.96*rmse_holt_pb,
               ses_hc$mean[1]+1.96*rmse_ses_hc,
               holt_hc$mean[1]+1.96*rmse_holt_hc)

# 95% interval by R:
lower_R = c(ses_pb$lower[1, "95%"], holt_pb$lower[1, "95%"],
            ses_hc$lower[1, "95%"], holt_hc$lower[1, "95%"])

upper_R = c(ses_pb$upper[1, "95%"], holt_pb$upper[1, "95%"],
            ses_hc$upper[1, "95%"], holt_hc$upper[1, "95%"])

kable(data.frame(
  Model = c("Paperback SES", "Paperback Holt", "Hardcover SES", "Hardcover Holt"),
  Lower_RMSE = lower_rmse,
  Upper_RMSE = upper_rmse,
  Lower_R = lower_R,
  Upper_R = upper_R
), digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
col.names = c("Model", "Lower (RMSE)", "Upper (RMSE)", "Lower (R)", "Upper (R)"))
```

The intervals based on the RMSE are slightly narrower than the R intervals. RMSE divides the SSE by $T$, whereas R divides by the degrees of freedom, $T-k$, where $k = 2$ for SES ($\alpha, \ell_0$) and $k = 4$ for Holt ($\alpha, \beta, \ell_0, b_0$). Since the series has only 30 observations, this difference is noticeable, especially for Holt's method. Neither interval accounts for the uncertainty in the parameter estimates, so both are likely too narrow.

## Question 5: Simulating using the state-space model formulation

In error-correction form, SES and Holt's method are state-space models with a single source of error:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + e_t, \qquad e_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \\
\ell_t &= \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + \alpha e_t \\
b_t &= b_{t-1} + \alpha\beta^* e_t
\end{aligned}
$$

For SES, $b_t = 0$ and $\beta^* = 0$.

```{r}
# Function to simulate from SES or Holt's method:
# n:   no. observations 
# par: parameters 
sim_fxn = function(n, par) {
  l     = par$l0
  b     = par$b0
  y     = numeric(n)
  level = numeric(n)
  
  for (t in 1:n) {
    e        = rnorm(1, 0, par$sigma)
    y[t]     = l + b + e                        # observation equation
    l        = l + b + par$alpha * e            # level
    b        = b + par$alpha * par$beta * e     # trend
    level[t] = l
  }
  list(y = ts(y), level = level)
}
```

### SES

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

# True parameters:
p_ses = list(alpha = 0.4, beta = 0, l0 = 3, b0 = 0, sigma = 0.5)

# Simulate:
sim_ses = sim_fxn(n = 100, par = p_ses)
y_ses = sim_ses$y

# Estimate with optim() and ses():
fit_sim = optim(par = c(0.5, y_ses[1]), 
                fn = my_sse, 
                y = y_ses,
                method = "L-BFGS-B", 
                lower = c(0.0001, -Inf), 
                upper = c(0.9999, Inf))
ses_sim = ses(y_ses)

kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("True value", "optim()", "ses()"),
  alpha = c(p_ses$alpha, fit_sim$par[1], ses_sim$model$par["alpha"]),
  l0 = c(p_ses$l0, fit_sim$par[2], ses_sim$model$par["l"]),
  sigma = c(p_ses$sigma, sqrt(fit_sim$value / (100 - 2)), sqrt(ses_sim$model$sigma2))
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The estimates from `optim()` and `ses()` are identical to 3 decimal places and both are close to the true parameter values. They do not match the true values exactly because they are based on a single simulated series, so some sampling variation is expected.

### Holt

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

# True parameters:
p_holt = list(alpha = 0.5, beta = 0.2, l0 = 10, b0 = 0.5, sigma = 1)
y_holt = sim_fxn(n = 100, par = p_holt)$y

holt_sim = holt(y_holt)

kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("True value", "holt()"),
  alpha = c(p_holt$alpha, holt_sim$model$par["alpha"]),
  beta = c(p_holt$alpha * p_holt$beta, holt_sim$model$par["beta"]),
  l0 = c(p_holt$l0, holt_sim$model$par["l"]),
  b0 = c(p_holt$b0, holt_sim$model$par["b"])
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

`holt()` reports $\beta$ on the error-correction scale, $\beta = \alpha\beta^*$, so the true value is $0.5 \times 0.2 = 0.1$. The estimates of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are reasonably close to the true values. The initial states are poorly estimated because only the first few observations carry information about them, and a higher starting level combined with a lower starting trend fits those observations almost equally well. This has little effect on the forecasts, which depend on the final level and trend rather than the starting values.

## Problem 1

**Question:** *How do different prediction intervals differ and what are their sources of uncertainty?*

I used the simulated SES series from Question 5, fitting each method to the first 80 observations and forecasting 10 steps ahead.

### A Bayesian SES sampler

Under the ETS(A,N,N) model, $y_t = \ell_{t-1} + e_t$ with $e_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ independent. Given $\alpha$, $\ell_0$ and $y_{1:t-1}$, the level $\ell_{t-1}$ is known, so $y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(\ell_{t-1}, \sigma^2)$. Writing the joint density as a product of these conditional densities gives the likelihood

$$
L(\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma; \boldsymbol{y}) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{\sigma}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{e_t}{\sigma}\right), \qquad e_t = y_t - \ell_{t-1},
$$

where $\phi$ is the standard normal density and $e_t$ depends on $(\alpha, \ell_0)$ through the SES recursion. The priors are $\alpha \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$ and flat priors on $\ell_0$ and $\log\sigma$.

A random walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm is used to sample from the posterior. The random walk steps are drawn from a multivariate normal distribution, which has support over the entire real line, whereas $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and $\sigma > 0$. Therefore, the parameters are mapped to the real line using

$$
\phi_1 = \text{logit}(\alpha), \qquad \phi_2 = \ell_0, \qquad \phi_3 = \log\sigma,
$$

and the random walk is performed over $\boldsymbol{\phi} = (\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3)$, with proposals $\boldsymbol{\phi}^* = \boldsymbol{\phi} + \boldsymbol{e}$. Since we sample $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ rather than $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma)$, the Jacobian of the transformation must be included in the log posterior. The flat prior on $\log\sigma$ is already defined on the transformed scale, so only $\alpha$ needs a Jacobian:

$$
\log p(\boldsymbol{\phi}) = \log L(\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma; \boldsymbol{y}) + \log\{\alpha(1-\alpha)\} + \text{const}.
$$

Since the proposal is symmetric, $\boldsymbol{\phi}^*$ is accepted with probability $\min\{1, \exp[\log p(\boldsymbol{\phi}^*) - \log p(\boldsymbol{\phi})]\}$. The steps are initially drawn from $\boldsymbol{e} \sim N(\boldsymbol{0}, 0.5^2\,\mathbf{I}_3)$. The first 3 000 iterations are a burn-in, and the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ of the transformed parameters is estimated from the last 1 500 of these. The retained draws then use $\boldsymbol{e} \sim N\left(\boldsymbol{0}, \frac{2.38^2}{3}\Sigma\right)$ (Roberts et al., 1997). The chain starts at the `ses()` estimates.

Each retained draw $(\alpha^{(j)}, \ell_0^{(j)}, \sigma^{(j)})$ is then used to compute $\ell_T^{(j)}$ and simulate one future path from the state-space model. This gives draws from the posterior predictive distribution of $y_{T+1}, \ldots, y_{T+h}$.

```{r}
# 1. SES log-likelihood: 
SES_Log_Likelihood = function(y, alpha, l0, sigma) {
  e   = ses_fxn(y, alpha, l0)$residuals
  out = sum(dnorm(e, 0, sigma, log = TRUE))
  if (!is.finite(out)) -Inf else out
}

# 2. Parameter transforms: 
to_real = function(theta) {
  c(qlogis(theta[1]), theta[2], log(theta[3]))
}

from_real = function(phi) {
  c(plogis(phi[1]), phi[2], exp(phi[3]))
}

# 3. Log posterior on the transformed scale (priors + Jacobian):
log_target = function(phi, y) {
  theta = from_real(phi)
  ll    = SES_Log_Likelihood(y, theta[1], theta[2], theta[3])
  if (!is.finite(ll)) return(-Inf)

  # Note: flat priors on l0 and log(sigma) only add a constant
  # Uniform(0, 1) prior on alpha x logit Jacobian:
  lp_alpha = plogis(phi[1], log.p = TRUE) + plogis(-phi[1], log.p = TRUE)

  ll + lp_alpha
}

# 4. Metropolis-Hastings loop:
mh_run = function(phi, jitters, y) {
  n         = nrow(jitters)
  cur       = log_target(phi, y)
  phi_draws = matrix(NA, n, 3)
  accepted  = logical(n)

  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    prop      = phi + jitters[i, ]
    prop_val  = log_target(prop, y)
    log_alpha = if (is.finite(prop_val)) min(0, prop_val - cur) else -Inf

    if (log(runif(1)) < log_alpha) {
      phi         = prop
      cur         = prop_val
      accepted[i] = TRUE
    }
    phi_draws[i, ] = phi
  }
  list(phi_draws = phi_draws, last = phi, accept_rate = mean(accepted))
}

# 5. Two-phase sampler: 
# Phase 1: burn-in with isotropic jitter, Sigma = covariance of later burn-in draws
# Phase 2: retained iterations with proposals ~ N(0, scale * Sigma)
MH_SES = function(y, init, iterations = 20000, burn = 3000, burn_sd = 0.5,
                  cov_frac = 0.5, scale = 2.38^2/3) {
  phi0 = to_real(init)

  # Phase 1:
  burn_jit = rmvnorm(burn, mean = rep(0, 3), sigma = burn_sd^2 * diag(3))
  b        = mh_run(phi0, burn_jit, y)
  keep     = seq.int(floor(burn * (1 - cov_frac)) + 1, burn)
  Sigma    = cov(b$phi_draws[keep, , drop = FALSE])

  # Phase 2:
  main_jit = rmvnorm(iterations, mean = rep(0, 3), sigma = scale * Sigma)
  m        = mh_run(b$last, main_jit, y)

  draws = t(apply(m$phi_draws, 1, from_real))
  colnames(draws) = c("alpha", "l0", "sigma")
  
  list(
    draws = draws, 
    burn_accept = b$accept_rate, 
    accept_rate = m$accept_rate)
}
```

As a check on my sample, I also fitted the same model in Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) to sample from the posterior. Stan uses the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), an adaptive form of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo that uses the gradient of the log posterior to propose new points. The `parameters` block restricts $\alpha$ to $(0, 1)$ and $\sigma$ to $(0, \infty)$, and Stan maps them to the real line and includes the Jacobian automatically. The `model` block runs the SES recursion, with $y_t \sim N(\ell_{t-1}, \sigma^2)$ at each step. The `generated quantities` block computes $\ell_T$ for each posterior draw and simulates one future path from the state-space model, which gives draws from the posterior predictive distribution of $y_{T+1}, \ldots, y_{T+h}$.

```{r}
# SES model written in Stan:
modelString = "
  data {
    int<lower=1> N;                   // number of observations
    vector[N] y;                      // time series
    int<lower=1> N_new;               // forecast horizon
  }

  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha;     // smoothing parameter
    real l0;                          // initial level
    real<lower=0> sigma;              // error standard deviation
  }

  model {
    real level = l0;

    // Priors (flat priors on l0 and sigma):
    alpha ~ uniform(0, 1);
    target += -log(sigma);            // flat prior on log(sigma)

    // Likelihood: one-step-ahead errors are iid N(0, sigma^2)
    for (t in 1:N) {
      y[t] ~ normal(level, sigma);
      level = level + alpha * (y[t] - level);
    }
  }

  generated quantities {
    real level_T;
    vector[N_new] y_new;

    // Final level for this draw:
    {
      real level = l0;
      for (t in 1:N) level = level + alpha * (y[t] - level);
      level_T = level;
    }

    // One future path from the state-space model:
    {
      real lev = level_T;
      for (h in 1:N_new) {
        real e = normal_rng(0, sigma);
        y_new[h] = lev + e;
        lev = lev + alpha * e;
      }
    }
  }
"
```

### Comparing prediction intervals

```{r}
#| cache: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

n_tr    = 80
h_max   = 10
y_train = window(y_ses, end = n_tr)
y_test  = window(y_ses, start = n_tr + 1, end = n_tr + h_max)

# 1. Normal intervals from ses():
fc_norm = ses(y_train, h = h_max, level = 95)

# 2. Manual normal intervals: 
a_hat        = fc_norm$model$par["alpha"]
res          = as.numeric(residuals(fc_norm))
sig2_hat     = sum(res^2)/(n_tr-2)
sd_h         = sqrt(sig2_hat*(1+a_hat^2*(1:h_max-1)))
manual_lower = fc_norm$mean-qnorm(0.975)*sd_h
manual_upper = fc_norm$mean+qnorm(0.975)*sd_h

# 3. Bootstrapped residuals: 
set.seed(2026)
B      = 5000
lev    = rep(fc_norm$mean[1], B)         
y_boot = matrix(NA, B, h_max)

for (k in 1:h_max) {
  e           = sample(res, size = B, replace = TRUE)
  y_boot[, k] = lev + e
  lev         = lev + a_hat * e
}
boot_pi = apply(y_boot, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

# 4. forecast():
fc_fboot = forecast(fc_norm$model, h = h_max, level = 95,
                    bootstrap = TRUE, simulate = TRUE, npaths = 5000)

# 5. Bayesian posterior predictive:
set.seed(2026)
init   = c(fc_norm$model$par["alpha"], fc_norm$model$par["l"], sqrt(fc_norm$model$sigma2))
fit_mh = MH_SES(y_train, init = init)

alpha_d = fit_mh$draws[, "alpha"]
l0_d    = fit_mh$draws[, "l0"]
sigma_d = fit_mh$draws[, "sigma"]

# One future path per posterior draw:
n_d = nrow(fit_mh$draws)
y_bayes = matrix(NA, n_d, h_max)
level_T = numeric(n_d)

for (j in 1:n_d) {
  lev_j      = ses_fxn(y_train, alpha_d[j], l0_d[j])$forecast  
  level_T[j] = lev_j
  
  for (k in 1:h_max) {
    e             = rnorm(1, 0, sigma_d[j])
    y_bayes[j, k] = lev_j + e
    lev_j         = lev_j + alpha_d[j] * e
  }
}
bayes_pi = apply(y_bayes, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

# 6. Bayesian posterior predictive (Stan):
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

stan_mod  = stan_model(model_code = modelString)
stan_data = list(N = n_tr, y = as.numeric(y_train), N_new = h_max)

stanFit = sampling(stan_mod,
                   data    = stan_data,
                   chains  = 3,
                   iter    = 6000,
                   warmup  = 1000,
                   seed    = 2026,
                   refresh = 0)

post_stan     = rstan::extract(stanFit)
bayes_pi_stan = apply(post_stan$y_new, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

# True values (from simulation):
lev_true = sim_ses$level[n_tr]
sd_true  = p_ses$sigma * sqrt(1 + p_ses$alpha^2 * (1:h_max - 1))
```

```{r}
pi_all = rbind(
  data.frame(method = "Normal: ses()", h = 1:h_max,
             lower  = as.numeric(fc_norm$lower), 
             upper  = as.numeric(fc_norm$upper)),
  data.frame(method = "Normal: by hand", h = 1:h_max,
             lower  = as.numeric(manual_lower), 
             upper  = as.numeric(manual_upper)),
  data.frame(method = "Bootstrap: own code", h = 1:h_max,
             lower  = boot_pi[1, ], 
             upper  = boot_pi[2, ]),
  data.frame(method = "Bootstrap: forecast()", h = 1:h_max,
             lower  = as.numeric(fc_fboot$lower), 
             upper  = as.numeric(fc_fboot$upper)),
  data.frame(method = "Bayesian: MH first principles", h = 1:h_max,
             lower  = bayes_pi[1, ], 
             upper  = bayes_pi[2, ]),
  data.frame(method = "Bayesian: Stan", h = 1:h_max,
             lower  = bayes_pi_stan[1, ],
             upper  = bayes_pi_stan[2, ]),
  data.frame(method = "True parameters", h = 1:h_max,
             lower  = lev_true - qnorm(0.975) * sd_true,
             upper  = lev_true + qnorm(0.975) * sd_true)
)
pi_all$width = pi_all$upper-pi_all$lower

# Interval widths at h = 1, 5 and 10:
width_tab = reshape(pi_all[pi_all$h %in% c(1, 5, 10), c("method", "h", "width")],
                    idvar = "method", timevar = "h", direction = "wide")
names(width_tab) = c("Method", "Width h=1", "Width h=5", "Width h=10")
kable(width_tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pi-compare
#| fig-cap: "95% prediction intervals for the simulated SES series from six approaches (pink), with the interval based on the true parameters (blue, dashed). Points are the test observations (not used for fitting)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

test_df = data.frame(h = 1:h_max, y = as.numeric(y_test))

# Interval with the true parameters (shown in every panel):
true_df = pi_all[pi_all$method == "True parameters", c("h", "lower", "upper")]

ggplot(data = pi_all[pi_all$method != "True parameters", ], mapping = aes(x = h)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), 
              fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = true_df, aes(y = lower), 
            col = "steelblue", linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(data = true_df, aes(y = upper), 
            col = "steelblue", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(data = test_df, 
             aes(y = y), 
             col = "deeppink") +
  facet_wrap(~method, ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of 95% prediction intervals.",
    x = "Forecast horizon (h)",
    y = "y"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Posterior summaries (own sampler vs Stan):
stan_sum = summary(stanFit, pars = c("alpha", "l0", "sigma"),
                   probs = c(0.025, 0.975))$summary
mh_sum   = t(apply(fit_mh$draws, 2, function(x) c(mean(x), quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975)))))

kable(data.frame(
  Parameter  = c("alpha", "l0", "sigma"),
  True       = c(p_ses$alpha, p_ses$l0, p_ses$sigma),
  MH_mean    = mh_sum[, 1],
  MH_lower   = mh_sum[, 2],
  MH_upper   = mh_sum[, 3],
  Stan_mean  = stan_sum[, "mean"],
  Stan_lower = stan_sum[, "2.5%"],
  Stan_upper = stan_sum[, "97.5%"]
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
col.names = c("Parameter", "True", "MH mean", "MH 2.5%", "MH 97.5%",
              "Stan mean", "Stan 2.5%", "Stan 97.5%"))

cat("MH acceptance rate (burn-in):", round(fit_mh$burn_accept, 2),
    " MH acceptance rate (retained):", round(fit_mh$accept_rate, 2),
    " Stan max Rhat:", round(max(stan_sum[, "Rhat"]), 3), "\n")
```

My Metropolis-Hastings sampler and Stan give almost identical posterior means and 95% credible intervals for all three parameters, which confirms that my sampler is correct. All three true values lie inside the credible intervals. The posterior for $\alpha$ is wide (roughly 0.34 to 0.65), so even with 80 observations there is considerable uncertainty about the smoothing parameter. This is the uncertainty that the plug-in intervals ignore. The initial level $\ell_0$ has the widest interval relative to its value, because only the first few observations carry information about it (as in Question 5).

**Error variance estimates.** Each method estimates $\sigma^2$ slightly differently:

```{r}
kable(data.frame(
  Estimate = c("$\\text{SSE}/(n-2)$ (`ses()`, normal intervals)",
               "$\\text{SSE}/n$ (implied by bootstrapping the residuals)",
               "$\\widehat{\\text{Var}}(e_t)$ (`var()`: divides by $n-1$, centres at $\\bar{e}$)",
               "$E(\\sigma^2 \\mid \\boldsymbol{y})$ (my MH sampler)",
               "$E(\\sigma^2 \\mid \\boldsymbol{y})$ (Stan)",
               "True $\\sigma^2$"),
  sigma2 = c(sig2_hat, sum(res^2) / n_tr, var(res),
             mean(sigma_d^2), mean(post_stan$sigma^2), p_ses$sigma^2)
), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE,
col.names = c("Estimate", "$\\hat{\\sigma}^2$"))
```

**What I found:**

-   The normal interval by hand reproduces `ses()` exactly, so `ses()` uses $\hat{\sigma}^2 = \text{SSE}/(n-2)$ and $\text{Var}(y_{T+h}) = \sigma^2[1+\alpha^2(h-1)]$.
-   The two bootstrap intervals differ at $h = 1$ (widths `r round(width_tab[3, 2], 2)` and `r round(width_tab[4, 2], 2)`) but are close to the normal interval at $h = 10$. At $h = 1$ a bootstrap interval is just the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the 80 residuals, so it depends on the few most extreme residuals and is very noisy. At longer horizons several resampled errors are added together, so this effect averages out. Bootstrapping only assumes *independent* errors, so it is safer when residuals are skewed or heavy-tailed, but it needs more data than the normal approach.
-   Both Bayesian intervals are wider than the normal interval at every horizon, and the difference grows with $h$ (from about 0.03 at $h=1$ to about 0.17 at $h=10$), because every future path uses a different draw of $(\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma)$. They are the only methods that include **parameter uncertainty**. My Metropolis-Hastings sampler and Stan give almost identical widths, which confirms that my sampler is correct.
-   Compared with the interval using the true parameters, the `ses()` interval is too narrow at $h=1$ but too wide at $h=10$. In this realisation $\hat{\sigma}$ is slightly too small and $\hat{\alpha}$ slightly too large, which shows that the plug-in interval depends on how good the parameter estimates happen to be.
-   None of the approaches includes uncertainty about the **choice of model** or whether the process will **keep behaving the same way**. This is why prediction intervals in practice are usually too narrow.

### Credible interval vs prediction interval

A **credible interval** describes uncertainty about an unknown quantity, here the current level $\ell_T$. A **prediction interval** describes uncertainty about a future *observation* $y_{T+h}$, so it also includes the future error $e_{T+h}$.

```{r}
ci_level = quantile(level_T, c(0.025, 0.975)) 
pi_y1    = bayes_pi[, 1]                      

kable(data.frame(
  Interval = c("Credible interval for $\\ell_T$",
               "Prediction interval for $y_{T+1}$"),
  Lower = as.numeric(c(ci_level[1], pi_y1[1])),
  Upper = as.numeric(c(ci_level[2], pi_y1[2]))
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The interval for the level is much narrower than the prediction interval, because most of the uncertainty about a single future observation comes from the noise $e_{T+1}$, not from estimating the level.

### Coverage of the normal intervals

A 95% prediction interval should contain the future value 95% of the time. I simulated 300 series ($n = 30$), fitted `ses()` and checked how often the 95% interval contained the true $y_{T+1}$ and $y_{T+10}$.

```{r}
set.seed(4)
cover = t(replicate(300, {
  sim    = sim_fxn(n = 40, par = p_ses)$y
  tr     = window(sim, end = 30)
  fc     = ses(tr, h = 10, level = 95)
  future = as.numeric(window(sim, start = 31))
  c(h1   = future[1] >= fc$lower[1] & future[1] <= fc$upper[1],
    h10  = future[10] >= fc$lower[10] & future[10] <= fc$upper[10])
}))
colMeans(cover)
```

The coverage is `r round(100 * mean(cover[, 1]), 1)`% at $h=1$ and `r round(100 * mean(cover[, 2]), 1)`% at $h=10$. With 300 replicates the Monte Carlo standard error is about 1.3%, so both are consistent with the nominal 95%. Even though the plug-in intervals ignore the uncertainty in $\hat{\alpha}$ and $\hat{\sigma}$, this has little effect on coverage here. One reason is that dividing the SSE by $n-2$ rather than $n$ already widens the intervals slightly. Another is that the errors really are normal and the model is correct, which is the best case for these intervals. With real data, where the model is only an approximation, the coverage would usually be lower.

# Time Series Regression

Time series regression models a response $y_t$ as a function of explanatory variables $\mathbf{x}_t$, combining the regression framework with the dependence structure of a time series. This lets us estimate and interpret the effect of $\mathbf{x}_t$ on $y_t$, and can improve forecasts beyond what the series' own past provides. Errors are usually serially correlated, which violates the independence assumption underlying ordinary least squares inference.

### Overview of the models

::: callout-warning
## Why ordinary regression is a problem

With autocorrelated errors, OLS estimates are still unbiased (if $x$ is exogenous) but no longer minimum variance, and the usual standard errors are wrong. Under positive autocorrelation they are typically too small, so OLS is overconfident: intervals are too narrow and variables can appear significant when they are not (spurious regression).
:::

The models differ in where the time dependence enters: through lags of the response, lags of the explanatory variables, or the errors (@tbl-tsr-models).

| Model                       | Equation                                                                                                     | Dependence through            | Use when                                                    |
|--------------|-----------------------------|--------------|---------------|
| ARMAX                       | $y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \dots + e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1} + \dots$                      | lagged response               | $y$ depends on its own past (e.g. a stock that accumulates) |
| Regression with ARMA errors | $y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \eta_t, \quad \phi(L)\eta_t = \theta(L)e_t$                                   | the errors                    | the effect of $x$ on the mean of $y$ is of interest         |
| Distributed lag             | $y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \beta_2 x_{t-1} + \dots + e_t$                                                | lagged explanatory variables  | the effect of $x$ takes time to work through                |
| VAR($p$)                    | $\mathbf{y}_t = \mathbf{c} + A_1\mathbf{y}_{t-1} + \dots + A_p\mathbf{y}_{t-p} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_t$ | lags of all variables         | the variables influence each other (feedback)               |
| GARMA                       | see below                                                                                                    | the errors, on the link scale | non-normal responses (counts, proportions)                  |

: Time series regression models. $e_t$ is white noise, $\phi(L)$ and $\theta(L)$ are the AR and MA polynomials in the lag operator $L$, and $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_t \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma)$. {#tbl-tsr-models}

In the ARMAX model $\beta_1$ is only the immediate effect of $x$, because $y_{t-1}$ carries part of its past effect. With ARMA errors, $\beta_1$ keeps its usual meaning as the effect of $x$ on the mean of $y$. This model is fitted with `arima(..., xreg = )` (maximum likelihood via the state-space form) or `gls()`. Each VAR equation can be fitted by OLS, and the model is used for Granger causality and impulse responses. GARMA extends ARMA errors to non-normal responses in the same way that GLMs extend linear regression:

$$
g(\mu_t) = \mathbf{x}_t'\boldsymbol{\beta} + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_j\left[g(y_{t-j}) - \mathbf{x}_{t-j}'\boldsymbol{\beta}\right] + \sum_{j=1}^{q} \theta_j\left[g(y_{t-j}) - g(\mu_{t-j})\right].
$$

In [Project 2](../projects/project-02.qmd) I used regression with SARIMA errors for dam levels with lagged sea surface temperature as a predictor. Lagged SST looked significant under OLS, but not once the errors were modelled.

## Example 4.1: Regression with autocorrelated errors

I reproduced the example in Section 4.1 of the regression chapter. The data are simulated from

$$
y_t = 1 - 4x_t + \eta_t, \qquad \eta_t = \phi\eta_{t-1} + e_t, \qquad e_t \sim N(0, 1), \quad \phi = 0.95,
$$

so the true slope is $-4$ and the errors are a very persistent AR(1).

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(dynlm)   # ARMAX models with L()
library(nlme)    # gls()

set.seed(12)
eta = numeric(100)

eta[1] = 10
x      = rnorm(100, 5, 1)
phi    = 0.95

# Auto-correlated errors:
for (i in 2:100) {
  eta[i] = phi*eta[i-1]+rnorm(1,0,1)
}

# Response, linear relationship + auto-correlated errors:
y = 1-4*x+eta
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex41-data
#| fig-cap: "Simulated data from Example 4.1: the response (left) and the AR(1) errors (right)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

ex41_long = data.frame(
  t = rep(1:100, 2),
  value = c(y, eta),
  series = factor(rep(c("Response", "AR(1) errors"), each = 100),
                  levels = c("Response", "AR(1) errors"))
)

ggplot(ex41_long, aes(x = t, y = value, col = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(data = data.frame(series = factor("AR(1) errors", levels = levels(ex41_long$series)),
                               yint = 0),
             aes(yintercept = yint), linetype = "dashed", col = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ series, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Response" = "deeppink", "AR(1) errors" = "purple")) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The errors start at $\eta_1 = 10$ and drift slowly back towards zero (@fig-ex41-data). With $\phi = 0.95$ they behave almost like a random walk, so the response wanders, even though it is a linear function of $x$ plus noise.

### Ordinary least squares

```{r}
a1 = lm(y ~ x)
summary(a1)
confint(a1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex41-acf
#| fig-cap: "ACF and PACF of the residuals from the OLS regression."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

p1 = ggAcf(resid(a1)) + labs(title = "ACF of OLS residuals") + theme_minimal()
p2 = ggPacf(resid(a1)) + labs(title = "PACF of OLS residuals") + theme_minimal()

p1 | p2
```

OLS gives a slope of `r round(coef(a1)[2], 3)` instead of $-4$, and the 95% confidence interval (`r round(confint(a1)[2, 1], 2)` to `r round(confint(a1)[2, 2], 2)`) misses the true value completely. OLS is unbiased on average but with errors this persistent one sample can land far from the truth. The standard error is calculated as if the errors were independent, so it is too small and OLS is overconfident. The residual ACF decays slowly and the PACF has a single large spike at lag 1 (@fig-ex41-acf). This is indicative of AR(1) errors.

### ARMAX: adding the lagged response

$$
y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \phi y_{t-1} + e_t.
$$

```{r}
y_ts = ts(y)
x_ts = ts(x)

arx1 = dynlm(y_ts ~ x_ts + L(y_ts, 1))
summary(arx1)

# Lagged response: 
y_lag = c(NA, y[-length(y)])
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex41-arx-acf
#| fig-cap: "ACF and PACF of the residuals from the ARMAX model."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

p1 = ggAcf(resid(arx1)) + labs(title = "ACF of ARMAX residuals") + theme_minimal()
p2 = ggPacf(resid(arx1)) + labs(title = "PACF of ARMAX residuals") + theme_minimal()

p1 | p2
```

The residual autocorrelation is much smaller but still present (@fig-ex41-arx-acf). The coefficient of $x$ (`r round(coef(arx1)[2], 3)`) is closer to $-4$, but it only measures the immediate effect of $x$, since $y_{t-1}$ carries part of the past effect of $x$. If $x$ increased by one unit permanently, the long-run effect would be $\hat{\beta}_1/(1-\hat{\phi}) = `r round(coef(arx1)[2] / (1 - coef(arx1)[3]), 2)`$, which is far from the true $-4$. Thus, the ARMAX model is misspecified. The data were generated with AR(1) errors, which also require the term $-\phi\beta_1 x_{t-1}$.

```{r}
# Autoregressive distributed lag model (x_{t-1} included):
x_lag = c(NA, x[-length(x)])
adl   = lm(y ~ y_lag + x + x_lag)
coef(adl)

c(coef_x_lag = unname(coef(adl)["x_lag"]),
  minus_phi_times_beta = unname(-coef(adl)["y_lag"] * coef(adl)["x"]))
```

The inclusion of $x_{t-1}$ results in the autoregressive distributed lag model. Its coefficients approximately satisfy the "common factor" restriction $\gamma = -\phi\beta_1$, where $\gamma$ is the coefficient of $x_{t-1}$. This is what the regression with AR(1) errors implies. Thus, the regression model with AR(1) errors is an ARMAX model that includes $x_{t-1}$ with its coefficient restricted to $-\phi \beta_1$.

### Regression with AR(1) errors

```{r}
a2 = arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = x)
a2
```

When we model the errors as an AR(1) process we obtain a slope of `r round(coef(a2)[3], 3)` with a standard error of `r round(sqrt(diag(a2$var.coef))[3], 3)`. This is very close to the true value of $-4$, and the standard error is much smaller when compared to OLS (0.495). The intercept is poorly estimated (`r round(coef(a2)["intercept"], 2)` instead of 1). Since $\hat{\phi}$ is close to 1 the errors behave almost as a random walk. Therefore, the intercept and the level of the error process are difficult to separate. In this simulation the errors did not start at their mean of 0 but at $\eta_1 = 10$. `arima()` estimates the model by maximum likelihood using the state-space form and the Kalman filter.

### Transforming the variables

Equation 1 in the notes motivates a transformation that removes the serial correlation. Defining $y_t^* = y_t - \phi y_{t-1}$ and $x_t^* = x_t - \phi x_{t-1}$ gives

$$
y_t^* = \beta_0(1-\phi) + \beta_1 x_t^* + e_t,
$$

where $e_t$ is white noise, so the OLS assumptions hold for the transformed model. Since $\phi$ is unknown, it is replaced by $\hat{\phi}$, the lag 1 autocorrelation of the OLS residuals, which makes this a feasible two-step estimator.

```{r}
phi_hat = acf(resid(a1), plot = FALSE)$acf[2]
phi_hat

y_star = y-phi_hat*y_lag
x_star = x-phi_hat*x_lag

a_star = lm(y_star ~ x_star)
summary(a_star)$coefficients
```

The estimated slope (`r round(coef(a_star)[2], 3)`) is close to the true value of $-4$, even though $\hat{\phi} = `r round(phi_hat, 2)`$ underestimates $\phi = 0.95$. However, the response is now $y_t^*$ as opposed to $y_t$, so $\beta_1$ describes how $y$ responds to $x$ after removing the carried-over error. When $\phi$ is close to 1 this is approximately the change in $y$ for a change in $x$. The intercept estimates $\beta_0(1-\phi)$, not $\beta_0$. Since the response differs, the AIC of this model cannot be compared with those of the other models.

### Generalised least squares

```{r}
m_gls = gls(y ~ x, correlation = corAR1(), method = "ML")
summary(m_gls)$tTable
coef(m_gls$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)  # estimated phi
```

`gls()` estimates the regression coefficients and the AR(1) parameter jointly by maximum likelihood. For a given $\phi$, the coefficients are the GLS estimator from the notes,

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (Z'V^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z'V^{-1}\mathbf{y}, \qquad V_{ij} \propto \phi^{|i-j|},
$$

where $Z$ is the design matrix and $V$ is the correlation structure implied by AR(1) errors. Iterating between estimating $\phi$ from the residuals and refitting with the updated $V$ (feasible GLS) gives very similar estimates. The estimates match those from `arima()` because both fit the same model by maximum likelihood.

### Minimising the independent SSE from first principles

For a regression with AR(1) errors, the independent errors are $e_t = (y_t - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_t) - \phi(y_{t-1} - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_{t-1})$, so the parameters can be estimated by minimising $\sum_{t=2}^{n} e_t^2$.

```{r}
# Sum of squared errors:
sse_ar1_err = function(par, y, x) {
  b0  = par[1]
  b1  = par[2]
  phi = par[3]
  eta = y-b0-b1*x                         # regression errors
  e   = eta[-1]-phi*eta[-length(eta)]         # independent errors
  sum(e^2)
}

fit_sse = optim(par = c(coef(a1), 0.5), fn = sse_ar1_err, y = y, x = x,
                method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 1000))

# Fitting arima() for comparison:
a2_css = arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = x, method = "CSS")

kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("My SSE + optim()", "arima(), CSS", "arima(), ML", "gls(), ML", "True value"),
  Intercept = c(fit_sse$par[1], coef(a2_css)["intercept"], coef(a2)["intercept"],
                coef(m_gls)[1], 1),
  Slope = c(fit_sse$par[2], coef(a2_css)[3], coef(a2)[3], coef(m_gls)[2], -4),
  phi = c(fit_sse$par[3], coef(a2_css)["ar1"], coef(a2)["ar1"],
          coef(m_gls$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE), 0.95)
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Minimising the sum of squared independent errors with `optim()` reproduces `arima(method = "CSS")` exactly, since both use the same conditional sum of squares criterion. All four methods agree closely on the slope and $\phi$, but differ on the intercept. CSS conditions on the first observation, so the starting value $\eta_1 = 10$ has no influence, and the intercept (1.134) is close to the true value of 1. Maximum likelihood (`arima()` and `gls()`) treats $\eta_1$ as a draw from the stationary distribution with mean 0, so the intercept is pushed up to 4.790 to account for the high starting value.

### Model comparison

```{r}
kable(data.frame(
  Model = c("a1: OLS", "arx1: ARMAX", "a2: AR(1) errors"),
  df = c(3, 4, 4),
  AIC = c(AIC(a1), AIC(arx1), AIC(a2))
), digits = 1, row.names = FALSE)
```

The regression with AR(1) errors has the lowest AIC (296.9, compared with 466.5 for the ARMAX model and 577.7 for OLS). This is expected, since it matches the data-generating process. The differences in AIC are large so the rankings hold even though the comparison is only approximate. The ARMAX model is fitted to 99 observations, whereas OLS and the exact maximum likelihood fit from `arima()` use all 100. In addition, `arima()` evaluates the likelihood through the state-space representation, which is not identical to the Gaussian likelihood `lm()` computes for independent errors.

### Forecasting with a regression with AR(1) errors

Forecasting $y_{T+h}$ requires values of $x_{T+h}$, which are not observed. Here $x$ is assumed to remain at its sample mean for the next 10 periods. The $h$-step forecast is then

$$
\hat{y}_{T+h} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_{T+h} + \hat{\phi}^h \hat{\eta}_T,
$$

so the error component decays geometrically from its last estimated value $\hat{\eta}_T$ towards zero, and the forecasts converge to the regression line $\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}$.

```{r}
x_future = rep(mean(x), 10)
fc_a2 = predict(a2, n.ahead = 10, newxreg = x_future)

fc_ex41 = data.frame(
  t = 101:110,
  fc = as.numeric(fc_a2$pred),
  lower = as.numeric(fc_a2$pred - 1.96 * fc_a2$se),
  upper = as.numeric(fc_a2$pred + 1.96 * fc_a2$se)
)
kable(fc_ex41, digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex41-fc
#| fig-cap: "Forecasts for the next 10 periods from the regression with AR(1) errors (x held at its mean), with 95% prediction intervals."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(t = 1:100, y = y), aes(x = t, y = y), col = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_ex41, aes(x = t, ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = fc_ex41, aes(x = t, y = fc), col = "deeppink") +
  labs(title = "Forecasts with AR(1) errors.", x = "Time", y = "y") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The prediction intervals widen quickly with the horizon (@fig-ex41-fc). This is due to $\hat{\phi}$ being close to 1, so the error process has long memory. The forecast variance $\sigma^2(1 + \phi^2 + \dots + \phi^{2(h-1)})$ keeps growing. These intervals are conditional on the future values of $x$ (assumed known). If $x$ was forecast as well, they would underestimate the uncertainty.

# State-Space Models

A state-space model has two equations: an observation equation that links what we observe to an unobserved state, and a state equation that describes how the state changes over time.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Observation:} \quad y_t &= F_t\theta_t + v_t, \qquad v_t \sim N(0, V) \\
\text{State:} \quad \theta_t &= G_t\theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad w_t \sim N(0, W) \\
\text{Prior:} \quad \theta_0 &\sim N(m_0, C_0)
\end{aligned}
$$

### Writing other models in state-space form

| Model                                | State $\theta_t$     | $F_t$      | $G_t$                                                    | Noise                                                                   |
|-------------|-------------|-------------|---------------|--------------------|
| Local level (random walk plus noise) | $\mu_t$              | $1$        | $1$                                                      | $V$, $W$                                                                |
| Local linear trend                   | $(\mu_t, \beta_t)'$  | $(1, 0)$   | $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$           | $V$, $W = \text{diag}(\sigma^2_\mu, \sigma^2_\beta)$                    |
| AR(2)                                | $(y_t, y_{t-1})'$    | $(1, 0)$   | $\begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & \phi_2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ | $V = 0$, $W = \text{diag}(\sigma^2, 0)$                                 |
| ARMA(1,1)                            | $(y_t, \theta e_t)'$ | $(1, 0)$   | $\begin{pmatrix} \phi & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$        | $V = 0$, $w_t = (e_t, \theta e_t)'$                                     |
| SES / ETS(A,N,N)                     | $\ell_t$             | $1$        | $1$                                                      | one error: $y_t = \ell_{t-1} + e_t$, $\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha e_t$ |
| Time-varying regression              | $(a_t, b_t)'$        | $(1, z_t)$ | $I_2$                                                    | $V$, $W = \text{diag}(\sigma^2_a, \sigma^2_b)$                          |

: Common models written as state-space models. {#tbl-ss-forms}

@tbl-ss-forms shows that very different models fit into the same two equations. An ARMA model is a state-space model with no observation noise ($V = 0$), where the state stores the recent values that the model needs to remember, while the structural models have noise in both equations.

Exponential smoothing models (ETS) are state-space models with a *single* source of error (the same $e_t$ drives the observation and the state), while the structural models in `dlm` have *two independent* sources of error ($v_t$ and $w_t$).

::: callout-note
## State-space models vs ARIMA models

-   **Stationarity.** ARIMA models need a stationary series (after differencing). State-space models do not: trend and seasonality are modelled directly as states that are allowed to change (random walks), so no differencing is needed.
-   **Modelling approach.** ARIMA models describe how $y_t$ depends on its own past and past shocks (a "black box" for the autocorrelation). Structural state-space models describe the components we believe generate the series (level, slope, season, regression effects), and each component can be estimated and plotted.
-   **Equivalence.** Every ARIMA model can be written in state-space form (this is how `arima()` computes the likelihood), and every linear structural model implies an ARIMA model for its differences. For example, the local level model implies $\Delta y_t = w_t + v_t - v_{t-1}$, an MA(1), so it is an ARIMA(0,1,1). The linear growth model gives an ARIMA(0,2,2).
-   **Practical advantages.** Missing observations, time-varying coefficients and filtered/smoothed estimates of the components all come out of the Kalman filter naturally.
:::

## Dynamic linear models with `dlm`

A dynamic linear model (DLM) is a linear, Gaussian state-space model. "Dynamic" means that the state $\theta_t$ (level, slope, seasonal effects, regression coefficients) is allowed to change over time.

### Random walk plus noise

The local level model has $F = G = 1$: the level follows a random walk and we observe it with noise.

```{r}
# Simulate from a random walk plus noise model:
rwpn = function(V = 0.8, W = 0.2, m0 = 0, C0 = 100, n = 100) {
  y = numeric(n)
  mu = numeric(n)
  for (i in 1:n) {
    if (i == 1) {
      mu[i] = rnorm(1, m0, sqrt(C0))        # initial state from the prior
    } else {
      mu[i] = rnorm(1, mu[i - 1], sqrt(W))  # state equation
    }
    y[i] = rnorm(1, mu[i], sqrt(V))         # observation equation
  }
  return(list(y = y, mu = mu))
}

set.seed(10)
sim_rw = rwpn()
y_rw = sim_rw$y
```

::: callout-warning
## `rnorm()` takes a standard deviation

In the original prac code `rnorm(1, m0, C0)` uses $C_0 = 100$ as a *standard deviation*, while the model treats $V$, $W$ and $C_0$ as *variances*. This is why the original simulated series started around $-11$. I used `sqrt()` so that the simulation matches the model that is fitted below.
:::

#### Defining the model

```{r}
# Define the model through its matrices:
mod_rwpn = dlm(FF = 1, V = 0.8, GG = 1, W = 0.2, m0 = 0, C0 = 100)
mod_rwpn

# Equivalent shortcut (dV and dW are the diagonal elements of V and W):
dlmModPoly(order = 1, dV = 0.8, dW = 0.2, C0 = 100)
```

`order = 1` gives a random walk for the state (local level model) and `order = 2` gives a random walk plus drift for the level (local linear trend). Individual matrices can be changed with the replacement functions:

```{r}
mod_copy = mod_rwpn
C0(mod_copy) = 80
C0(mod_copy)
```

#### Kalman filter and smoother

```{r}
filt_rw = dlmFilter(y_rw, mod_rwpn)
names(filt_rw)

# Note: m has one more element than y (first element is m0)
length(filt_rw$m)

# Filtered variances C_t (from SVD stored by dlm):
C_rw = unlist(dlmSvd2var(filt_rw$U.C, filt_rw$D.C))

# Kalman smoother:
smooth_rw = dlmSmooth(filt_rw)
S_rw = unlist(dlmSvd2var(smooth_rw$U.S, smooth_rw$D.S))
```

`dlmFilter()` returns the filtered states `m` ($\theta_t \mid y_{1:t} \sim N(m_t, C_t)$), the one-step-ahead state predictions `a` ($\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(a_t, R_t)$), the one-step-ahead forecasts of the observations `f`, and the variances in SVD form (`U.C`, `D.C`, `U.R`, `D.R`). `dlmSvd2var()` turns these back into variance matrices.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rwpn-filter
#| fig-cap: "Simulated random walk plus noise data (grey points), true level (black), filtered level with 95% interval (pink) and smoothed level (blue)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

rw_df = data.frame(
  t = 1:100,
  y = y_rw,
  mu = sim_rw$mu,
  filtered = filt_rw$m[-1],
  lower = filt_rw$m[-1] - 1.96 * sqrt(C_rw[-1]),
  upper = filt_rw$m[-1] + 1.96 * sqrt(C_rw[-1]),
  smoothed = smooth_rw$s[-1]
)

ggplot(data = rw_df, mapping = aes(x = t)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(y = y), col = "grey60", size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mu), col = "black") +
  geom_line(aes(y = filtered), col = "deeppink") +
  geom_line(aes(y = smoothed), col = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Filtered and smoothed level for a random walk plus noise.",
    x = "Time",
    y = "y"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The filtered level (pink) only uses observations up to time $t$, so it reacts to changes with a delay. The smoothed level (blue) also uses later observations, so it is smoother and closer to the true level (black) (@fig-rwpn-filter). The smoothed variances are smaller than the filtered ones (average `r round(mean(S_rw[-1]), 3)` vs `r round(mean(C_rw[-1]), 3)`), except at the end of the series where they are the same: at $t = T$ there is no future information to add.

#### Maximum likelihood

If $V$ and $W$ are unknown, the Kalman filter gives the likelihood through the one-step-ahead prediction errors, and `dlmMLE()` passes it to `optim()`. The variances are estimated on the log scale so they stay positive.

```{r}
# Function to build model from log parameters:
build_rw = function(par) {
  dlmModPoly(order = 1, dV = exp(par[1]), dW = exp(par[2]))
}

# Maximise the likelihood:
fit_rw = dlmMLE(y_rw, parm = c(0, 0), build = build_rw, hessian = TRUE)
fit_rw$convergence  # 0 = converged

# Estimates with 95% CIs (log scale, then back-transformed):
se_log = sqrt(diag(solve(fit_rw$hessian)))
kable(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("V", "W"),
  True = c(0.8, 0.2),
  Estimate = exp(fit_rw$par),
  Lower = exp(fit_rw$par - 1.96 * se_log),
  Upper = exp(fit_rw$par + 1.96 * se_log)
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The confidence intervals are wide, especially for $W$. With 100 observations it is hard to separate "the level moved" from "the observation was noisy", because both create variation in $y_t$. The signal-to-noise ratio $W/V$ is what matters for the filter.

#### Forecasting

For a random walk plus noise model, the forecast is flat at the last filtered level (just like SES), and the uncertainty grows linearly with the horizon.

```{r}
mod_rw_fit = build_rw(fit_rw$par)
filt_rw_fit = dlmFilter(y_rw, mod_rw_fit)
fc_rw = dlmForecast(filt_rw_fit, nAhead = 10)

str(fc_rw, max.level = 1)
```

`dlmForecast()` returns forecasts of the state (`a`, with variances `R`) and of the observations (`f`, with variances `Q`). Note that $Q_t = R_t + V$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rwpn-forecast
#| fig-cap: "Ten-step forecasts for the random walk plus noise model: 95% interval for the level (dark pink, uses R) and 95% prediction interval for new observations (light pink, uses Q)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

fc_df = data.frame(
  t = 101:110,
  f = as.numeric(fc_rw$f),
  lev_lo = as.numeric(fc_rw$a) - 1.96 * sqrt(unlist(fc_rw$R)),
  lev_hi = as.numeric(fc_rw$a) + 1.96 * sqrt(unlist(fc_rw$R)),
  y_lo = as.numeric(fc_rw$f) - 1.96 * sqrt(unlist(fc_rw$Q)),
  y_hi = as.numeric(fc_rw$f) + 1.96 * sqrt(unlist(fc_rw$Q))
)
obs_df = data.frame(t = 61:100, y = y_rw[61:100], m = filt_rw_fit$m[62:101])

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_df, aes(x = t, ymin = y_lo, ymax = y_hi), fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_df, aes(x = t, ymin = lev_lo, ymax = lev_hi), fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = fc_df, aes(x = t, y = f), col = "deeppink") +
  geom_point(data = obs_df, aes(x = t, y = y), col = "grey50", size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = obs_df, aes(x = t, y = m), col = "deeppink") +
  labs(
    title = "Forecasts from the random walk plus noise model.",
    x = "Time",
    y = "y"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: callout-important
## State interval vs prediction interval

The original prac plotted $a_t \pm 1.96\sqrt{R_t}$. That is an interval for the future *level*, not for future *observations*. A prediction interval for $y_{T+h}$ must use $Q_t = R_t + V$, which also includes the observation noise. In @fig-rwpn-forecast the prediction interval is much wider.
:::

### Nile data: local level model

```{r}
# Read in data:
data(Nile)
# View(Nile)

# Local level model with unknown variances:
build_nile = function(par) {
  dlmModPoly(order = 1, dV = exp(par[1]), dW = exp(par[2]))
}
fit_nile = dlmMLE(Nile, parm = c(log(10000), log(1000)), build = build_nile)
var_nile = exp(fit_nile$par)
names(var_nile) = c("V", "W")
var_nile

mod_nile = build_nile(fit_nile$par)
filt_nile = dlmFilter(Nile, mod_nile)
smooth_nile = dlmSmooth(filt_nile)
fc_nile = dlmForecast(filt_nile, nAhead = 10)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-nile
#| fig-cap: "Annual flow of the Nile at Aswan (grey), filtered level (pink), smoothed level with 95% interval (blue) and 10-year forecasts with 95% prediction intervals. The dashed line marks 1898, when construction of the Aswan dam started."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

S_nile = unlist(dlmSvd2var(smooth_nile$U.S, smooth_nile$D.S))
nile_df = data.frame(
  year = as.numeric(time(Nile)),
  flow = as.numeric(Nile),
  filtered = as.numeric(dropFirst(filt_nile$m)),
  smoothed = as.numeric(dropFirst(smooth_nile$s)),
  s_lo = as.numeric(dropFirst(smooth_nile$s)) - 1.96 * sqrt(S_nile[-1]),
  s_hi = as.numeric(dropFirst(smooth_nile$s)) + 1.96 * sqrt(S_nile[-1])
)
nile_fc_df = data.frame(
  year = 1971:1980,
  f = as.numeric(fc_nile$f),
  lo = as.numeric(fc_nile$f) - 1.96 * sqrt(unlist(fc_nile$Q)),
  hi = as.numeric(fc_nile$f) + 1.96 * sqrt(unlist(fc_nile$Q))
)

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = nile_df, aes(x = year, ymin = s_lo, ymax = s_hi), fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = nile_df, aes(x = year, y = flow), col = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = nile_df, aes(x = year, y = filtered), col = "deeppink") +
  geom_line(data = nile_df, aes(x = year, y = smoothed), col = "steelblue") +
  geom_ribbon(data = nile_fc_df, aes(x = year, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = nile_fc_df, aes(x = year, y = f), col = "deeppink") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1898, linetype = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Local level model for the Nile.",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Flow (100 million cubic metres)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The estimated observation variance ($\hat{V} = `r round(var_nile["V"])`$) is about $`r round(var_nile["V"] / var_nile["W"])`$ times larger than the level variance ($\hat{W} = `r round(var_nile["W"])`$), so the filter changes the level slowly and treats most year-to-year variation as noise. The smoothed level (@fig-nile) shows the drop in flow around 1898 very clearly. Because the smoother uses future observations, it starts dropping *before* 1898, while the filtered level only reacts afterwards.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nile-res
#| fig-cap: "Standardised one-step-ahead prediction errors for the local level model of the Nile: ACF and normal Q-Q plot."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

res_nile = residuals(filt_nile, sd = FALSE)  # standardised innovations

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(res_nile, main = "ACF")
qqnorm(res_nile, col = "deeppink", main = "Normal Q-Q plot")
qqline(res_nile)
```

```{r}
Box.test(res_nile, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 2)
```

The standardised prediction errors are the model's residuals. If the model is adequate they should look like independent $N(0,1)$ values. Here the ACF and the Ljung-Box test (p = `r round(Box.test(res_nile, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 2)$p.value, 3)`) are used to check for leftover autocorrelation (@fig-nile-res).

### Nile data: local linear trend model

`dlmModPoly()` with its default `order = 2` gives the local linear trend (linear growth) model, which adds a slope that can also change over time.

```{r}
#| warning: false

build_llt = function(par) {
  dlmModPoly(order = 2, dV = exp(par[1]), dW = exp(par[2:3]))
}
fit_llt = dlmMLE(Nile, parm = c(log(15000), log(1000), log(10)), build = build_llt)
var_llt = exp(fit_llt$par)
names(var_llt) = c("V", "W_level", "W_slope")
var_llt

# Compare with local level model (dlmMLE returns -logL):
kable(data.frame(
  Model = c("Local level", "Local linear trend"),
  Parameters = c(2, 3),
  neg_loglik = c(fit_nile$value, fit_llt$value),
  AIC = c(2 * fit_nile$value + 2 * 2, 2 * fit_llt$value + 2 * 3)
), digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

The estimated slope variance is very small, so the slope hardly changes, and adding it does not improve the fit enough to justify the extra parameter. This makes sense, since the Nile has a level shift, not a trend. (The comparison is only approximate, because the two models have a different number of diffuse initial states, which affects the first few likelihood terms.)

### Missing observations

```{r}
# Remove 1910-1915:
nile_na = Nile
nile_na[40:45] = NA

fit_na = dlmMLE(nile_na, parm = c(log(10000), log(1000)), build = build_nile)
filt_na = dlmFilter(nile_na, build_nile(fit_na$par))
C_na = unlist(dlmSvd2var(filt_na$U.C, filt_na$D.C))
C_full = unlist(dlmSvd2var(filt_nile$U.C, filt_nile$D.C))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-nile-missing
#| fig-cap: "Filtered level with 95% intervals for the full Nile series (blue) and with 1910–1915 removed (pink)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

na_df = data.frame(
  year = rep(1871:1970, 2),
  series = rep(c("Full series", "1910-1915 missing"), each = 100),
  m = c(as.numeric(dropFirst(filt_nile$m)), as.numeric(dropFirst(filt_na$m))),
  se = c(sqrt(C_full[-1]), sqrt(C_na[-1]))
)
na_df = na_df[na_df$year >= 1895 & na_df$year <= 1935, ]

ggplot(data = na_df, mapping = aes(x = year, y = m, colour = series, fill = series)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = m - 1.96 * se, ymax = m + 1.96 * se), alpha = 0.25, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(year = 1895:1935, flow = as.numeric(window(Nile, 1895, 1935))),
             aes(x = year, y = flow), inherit.aes = FALSE, col = "grey50", size = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Full series" = "steelblue", "1910-1915 missing" = "deeppink")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Full series" = "steelblue", "1910-1915 missing" = "deeppink")) +
  labs(
    title = "Filtering with missing observations.",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Flow",
    colour = "",
    fill = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

When an observation is missing there is nothing to update with: the Kalman gain is zero, so $m_t = a_t$ and $C_t = R_t = C_{t-1} + W$. The filtered level stays flat through the gap and the interval widens by $W$ every year (@fig-nile-missing). As soon as observations return, the interval shrinks back.

### Seasonality: basic structural model for CO$_2$

The basic structural model adds 11 seasonal states (12 monthly effects that sum to zero) to the local linear trend:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \mu_t + s_t + v_t, & v_t \sim N(0, V) \\
\mu_t &= \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_t, & w_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_w) \\
\beta_t &= \beta_{t-1} + \gamma_t, & \gamma_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\gamma) \\
s_t &= -\sum_{j=1}^{S-1} s_{t-j} + \delta_t, & \delta_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\delta)
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-co2
#| fig-cap: "Monthly atmospheric CO2 concentration at Mauna Loa, 1959–1997."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Read in data:
data(co2)

co2_df = data.frame(month = as.numeric(time(co2)), ppm = as.numeric(co2))

ggplot(data = co2_df, mapping = aes(x = month, y = ppm)) +
  geom_line(col = "deeppink") +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly CO2 concentration (1959–1997).",
    x = "Month",
    y = "CO2 (ppm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

@fig-co2 shows a steady upward trend and a regular yearly cycle with a constant amplitude (additive seasonality).

```{r}
# Structure: 2 trend states + 11 seasonal states = 13 states:
m_s1 = dlmModPoly() + dlmModSeas(12)
dim(m_s1$GG)
diag(W(m_s1))  # default: level var 0, slope var 1, one seasonal var 1
```

Only three states get noise: the level, the slope and the current seasonal effect. The other seasonal states are just the previous effects shifted along.

```{r}
#| cache: true

# Function to build model from log variances:
lik_s1 = function(p) {
  mod = dlmModPoly() + dlmModSeas(12)
  Wm = W(mod)
  diag(Wm)[1:3] = exp(p[1:3])  # level, slope and seasonal variances
  W(mod) = Wm
  V(mod) = exp(p[4])           # observation variance
  return(mod)
}

mle_s1 = dlmMLE(co2, parm = c(0, 0, 0, 0), build = lik_s1)
```

```{r}
mle_s1$convergence

var_s1 = exp(mle_s1$par)
names(var_s1) = c("level", "slope", "seasonal", "observation")
signif(var_s1, 3)

fit_s1 = lik_s1(mle_s1$par)
filt_s1 = dlmFilter(co2, fit_s1)
```

The slope and seasonal variances are tiny compared to the level and observation variances. The trend and the seasonal pattern change very slowly, while the level absorbs the short-term movements.

```{r}
#| label: fig-co2-filter
#| fig-cap: "CO2 data (grey) with the filtered level (blue), the filtered level plus seasonal effect (orange) and the one-step-ahead fitted values (pink). Right: the first three years."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Full series"
#|   - "1959–1961"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

co2_filt_df = data.frame(
  month = as.numeric(time(co2)),
  co2 = as.numeric(co2),
  level = as.numeric(dropFirst(filt_s1$m[, 1])),
  level_season = as.numeric(dropFirst(filt_s1$m[, 1])) + as.numeric(dropFirst(filt_s1$m[, 3])),
  fitted = as.numeric(filt_s1$f)
)

co2_plot = function(df) {
  ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = month)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = co2, colour = "Observed")) +
    geom_line(aes(y = level, colour = "Level")) +
    geom_line(aes(y = level_season, colour = "Level + season")) +
    geom_line(aes(y = fitted, colour = "Fitted (one-step)"), linetype = 2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = "grey50", "Level" = "steelblue",
                                   "Level + season" = "orange", "Fitted (one-step)" = "deeppink")) +
    labs(x = "Month", y = "CO2 (ppm)", colour = "") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}

co2_plot(co2_filt_df) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(310, 370))
co2_plot(co2_filt_df[1:36, ])
```

The prior is very vague ($m_0 = 0$, $C_0 = 10^7 I$ for all 13 states). After the first observation the filter knows that level + season ≈ 315, but it cannot tell how much of that is level and how much is the January effect. Until it has seen roughly a year of data, the seasonal effects are not identified, so the filtered level and seasonal states jump around wildly (right panel of @fig-co2-filter). After about a year the filter has learned the seasonal pattern and the level settles down.

The one-step-ahead forecasts `filt_s1$f` are the fitted values. After the first year they lie almost on top of the observations.

#### Forecasts for the next five years

```{r}
fc_s1 = dlmForecast(filt_s1, nAhead = 60)

co2_fc_df = data.frame(
  month = as.numeric(tail(time(co2), 1)) + (1:60) / 12,
  f = as.numeric(fc_s1$f),
  lo = as.numeric(fc_s1$f) - 1.96 * sqrt(unlist(fc_s1$Q)),
  hi = as.numeric(fc_s1$f) + 1.96 * sqrt(unlist(fc_s1$Q))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-co2-fc
#| fig-cap: "Five-year forecasts of CO2 from the basic structural model with 95% prediction intervals (data from 1988 onwards shown)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = co2_df[co2_df$month >= 1988, ], aes(x = month, y = ppm), col = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(data = co2_fc_df, aes(x = month, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = co2_fc_df, aes(x = month, y = f), col = "deeppink") +
  labs(
    title = "CO2 forecasts for 1998–2002.",
    x = "Month",
    y = "CO2 (ppm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The forecasts in @fig-co2-fc continue the upward trend and repeat the seasonal pattern, with intervals that widen over the five years. This can be explained by the uncertainty about the level and slope accumulating.

### Seasonality with trigonometric terms

Instead of 11 seasonal states, the seasonal pattern can be built from sine and cosine waves (harmonics). The $j$th harmonic has frequency $\omega_j = 2\pi j / s$ and needs two states. With $q$ harmonics there are $2q$ seasonal states, so $q = 1$ gives a pure sine-shaped season with only 2 states. This links directly to the harmonics in [Spectral Analysis](../section-1/section-1.qmd#spectral-analysis) in Section 1.

```{r}
# Check the structure for q = 1:
m_trig = dlmModPoly() + dlmModTrig(s = 12, q = 1)
m_trig$GG
```

The $2 \times 2$ block in `GG` rotates the harmonic by $\omega_1 = 2\pi/12$ each month ($\cos(\pi/6) = 0.866$, $\sin(\pi/6) = 0.5$).

```{r}
#| cache: true

# Function to build model with q harmonics (seasonal states share one variance):
build_trig = function(q) {
  function(p) {
    mod = dlmModPoly() + dlmModTrig(s = 12, q = q)
    k = nrow(mod$GG)
    Wm = W(mod)
    diag(Wm) = c(exp(p[1]), exp(p[2]), rep(exp(p[3]), k - 2))
    W(mod) = Wm
    V(mod) = exp(p[4])
    return(mod)
  }
}

# Fit q = 1, 2, 3:
fits_trig = lapply(1:3, function(q) dlmMLE(co2, parm = c(0, 0, 0, 0), build = build_trig(q)))
```

```{r}
trig_tab = data.frame(
  Model = c("dlmModSeas (11 seasonal states)", paste0("Trigonometric, q = ", 1:3)),
  Seasonal_states = c(11, 2 * (1:3)),
  neg_loglik = c(mle_s1$value, sapply(fits_trig, function(f) f$value))
)
trig_tab$AIC = 2 * trig_tab$neg_loglik + 2 * 4  # 4 variance parameters in each model
kable(trig_tab, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-co2-seasonal
#| fig-cap: "Filtered seasonal effect for 1990–1997 from the dummy seasonal model and from trigonometric models with one and two harmonics."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Function to extract seasonal component (F without trend states x filtered seasonal states):
seas_comp = function(filt, mod) {
  as.numeric(dropFirst(filt$m)[, -(1:2)] %*% mod$FF[1, -(1:2)])
}

mod_q1 = build_trig(1)(fits_trig[[1]]$par)
mod_q2 = build_trig(2)(fits_trig[[2]]$par)

seas_df = data.frame(
  month = rep(as.numeric(time(co2)), 3),
  model = rep(c("Dummy seasonal", "Trig, q = 1", "Trig, q = 2"), each = length(co2)),
  effect = c(seas_comp(filt_s1, fit_s1),
             seas_comp(dlmFilter(co2, mod_q1), mod_q1),
             seas_comp(dlmFilter(co2, mod_q2), mod_q2))
)
seas_df = seas_df[seas_df$month >= 1990, ]

ggplot(data = seas_df, mapping = aes(x = month, y = effect, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Dummy seasonal" = "grey40", "Trig, q = 1" = "steelblue",
                                 "Trig, q = 2" = "deeppink")) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated seasonal effect.",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Seasonal effect (ppm)",
    colour = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
