The CO$_2$ seasonal cycle is not a perfect sine wave: concentrations rise slowly over the northern winter and fall quickly during the growing season. One harmonic forces a symmetric shape, while the second harmonic lets the peak and trough be asymmetric (@fig-co2-seasonal). The table shows by how much the likelihood improves when harmonics are added. Every model has the same four variance parameters, so the AIC comparison here is effectively a likelihood comparison (with the same caveat about diffuse initial states as before).

#### Constant seasonal effect, and the link to harmonic regression

Setting the seasonal variance to zero makes the seasonal pattern constant over time (the harmonics still rotate, but their amplitudes no longer change).

```{r}
#| cache: true

build_trig_const = function(q) {
  function(p) {
    mod = dlmModPoly() + dlmModTrig(s = 12, q = q)
    k = nrow(mod$GG)
    Wm = W(mod)
    diag(Wm) = c(exp(p[1]), exp(p[2]), rep(0, k - 2))  # no noise in the seasonal states
    W(mod) = Wm
    V(mod) = exp(p[3])
    return(mod)
  }
}
fit_const = dlmMLE(co2, parm = c(0, 0, 0), build = build_trig_const(2))
c(neg_loglik_constant = fit_const$value, neg_loglik_changing = fits_trig[[2]]$value)
```

If the level and slope variances are also zero, every state is deterministic and the model becomes a linear regression with a linear trend and harmonic terms:

$$
y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{j=1}^{2}\left[a_j \cos(\omega_j t) + b_j \sin(\omega_j t)\right] + v_t.
$$

```{r}
tt = 1:length(co2)

# Harmonic regression:
lm_harm = lm(co2 ~ tt + sin(2 * pi * tt / 12) + cos(2 * pi * tt / 12) +
               sin(4 * pi * tt / 12) + cos(4 * pi * tt / 12))

# Same model as a DLM with all state variances = 0:
mod_det = dlmModPoly(order = 2, dV = 1, dW = c(0, 0)) + dlmModTrig(s = 12, q = 2, dV = 0, dW = 0)
filt_det = dlmFilter(co2, mod_det)
m_T = filt_det$m[length(co2) + 1, ]

kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Slope", "Fitted value at the last month"),
  lm = c(coef(lm_harm)["tt"], fitted(lm_harm)[length(co2)]),
  dlm = c(m_T[2], sum(mod_det$FF * m_T)),
  row.names = NULL
), digits = 5, row.names = FALSE)
```

The Kalman filter with a vague prior and no state noise gives the same slope and the same fitted value as `lm()`: the filter is just computing least squares recursively.

```{r}
#| label: fig-harm-res
#| fig-cap: "ACF of the residuals from the harmonic regression for CO2."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

acf(resid(lm_harm), main = "Harmonic regression residuals", lag.max = 48)
```

The residuals of the harmonic regression are strongly autocorrelated (@fig-harm-res): a straight line and a fixed seasonal pattern do not describe 39 years of CO$_2$ well. This is the main argument for the dynamic (state-space) version, where the level, slope and seasonal pattern can drift.

# The Kalman Filter

## The Kalman filter from first principles

The function below implements the three steps for a univariate observation and a state of any dimension. $F_t$ and $G_t$ can be given either as fixed matrices or as functions of $t$ (for time-varying models), and missing values (`NA`) are handled by skipping the update. The output is stored the same way as in `dlmFilter()`: row 1 of `m` (and element 1 of `C`) is the prior at time 0.

```{r}
# Function to code the Kalman filter from first principles: 
kalman_filter = function(y, FF, GG, V, W, m0, C0) {
  n = length(y)
  p = length(m0)

  # Define F_t and G_t:
  get_F = if (is.function(FF)) FF else function(t) FF
  get_G = if (is.function(GG)) GG else function(t) GG

  a = matrix(NA, n, p)        # prior means
  R = vector("list", n)
  m = matrix(NA, n + 1, p)    # posterior means
  C = vector("list", n + 1)
  f = Q = e = rep(NA, n)      # forecasts

  m[1, ] = m0                
  C[[1]] = as.matrix(C0)
  loglik = 0

  for (t in 1:n) {
    Ft = matrix(get_F(t), nrow = 1)
    Gt = as.matrix(get_G(t))

    # 1. Predict the state:
    a[t, ] = Gt %*% m[t, ]
    R[[t]] = Gt %*% C[[t]] %*% t(Gt) + W

    # 2. Predict the observation:
    f[t] = drop(Ft %*% a[t, ])
    Q[t] = drop(Ft %*% R[[t]] %*% t(Ft)) + V

    # 3. Update with y_t:
    if (is.na(y[t])) {
      # No observation = no update
      m[t + 1, ] = a[t, ]
      C[[t + 1]] = R[[t]]
    } else {
      e[t] = y[t] - f[t]                    # one-step-ahead prediction error
      K = R[[t]] %*% t(Ft) / Q[t]           # Kalman gain 
      m[t + 1, ] = a[t, ] + drop(K) * e[t]
      C[[t + 1]] = R[[t]] - K %*% Ft %*% R[[t]]
      loglik = loglik + dnorm(y[t], f[t], sqrt(Q[t]), log = TRUE)
    }
  }

  list(m = m, C = C, a = a, R = R, f = f, Q = Q, e = e, loglik = loglik)
}
```

```{r}
# Function to code the Kalman smoother from first principles: 
kalman_smoother = function(kf, GG) {
  n = nrow(kf$a)
  p = ncol(kf$a)
  get_G = if (is.function(GG)) GG else function(t) GG

  s = matrix(NA, n + 1, p)    # smoothed means
  S = vector("list", n + 1)

  # At last time point smoothed:
  s[n + 1, ] = kf$m[n + 1, ]
  S[[n + 1]] = kf$C[[n + 1]]

  # Backwards recursion:
  for (t in n:1) {
    Gt = as.matrix(get_G(t))
    J = kf$C[[t]] %*% t(Gt) %*% solve(kf$R[[t]])   # smoother gain
    s[t, ] = kf$m[t, ] + J %*% (s[t + 1, ] - kf$a[t, ])
    S[[t]] = kf$C[[t]] + J %*% (S[[t + 1]] - kf$R[[t]]) %*% t(J)
  }

  list(s = s, S = S)
}
```

::: callout-tip
## Indexing

$G_t$ is used in the *prediction* step for $\theta_t$ (moving from $t-1$ to $t$), and $F_t$ is used to predict $y_t$ from $\theta_t$. Using $G_{t-1}$ or $F_{t-1}$ by mistake is easy and gives wrong results that still look reasonable. The extra row for time 0 in `m` is another place where off-by-one errors happen.
:::

### Checking my filter against `dlm`: the Nile data

I maximise my log-likelihood over $\log V$ and $\log W$ with `optim()`, using the same vague prior as `dlmModPoly()` ($m_0 = 0$, $C_0 = 10^7$).

```{r}
# Function to calculate negative log-likelihood of local level model:
nile_nll = function(par) {
  -kalman_filter(Nile, FF = 1, GG = 1, V = exp(par[1]), W = exp(par[2]),
                 m0 = 0, C0 = 1e7)$loglik
}

fit_own_nile = optim(par = c(log(10000), log(1000)), fn = nile_nll,
                     method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)

V_own = exp(fit_own_nile$par[1])
W_own = exp(fit_own_nile$par[2])

# 95% CIs from Hessian:
se_own = sqrt(diag(solve(fit_own_nile$hessian)))

kable(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("V", "W"),
  `My filter + optim()` = c(V_own, W_own),
  Lower = exp(fit_own_nile$par - 1.96 * se_own),
  Upper = exp(fit_own_nile$par + 1.96 * se_own),
  `dlmMLE()` = var_nile,
  check.names = FALSE
), digits = 1, row.names = FALSE)
```

My filter and `dlmMLE()` give the same estimates ($\hat{V} \approx `r round(V_own)`$, $\hat{W} \approx `r round(W_own)`$), which are also the values reported for the Nile local level model by Durbin and Koopman (2012).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nile-check
#| tbl-cap: "Largest absolute differences between my Kalman filter/smoother and `dlm`."

# Own filter and smoother at own estimates:
kf_nile = kalman_filter(Nile, FF = 1, GG = 1, V = V_own, W = W_own, m0 = 0, C0 = 1e7)
ks_nile = kalman_smoother(kf_nile, GG = 1)

# dlm with the same parameters:
mod_check    = dlmModPoly(order = 1, dV = V_own, dW = W_own)
filt_check   = dlmFilter(Nile, mod_check)
smooth_check = dlmSmooth(filt_check)

# Forecasts: append 10 NAs to series and run own filter again:
kf_fc    = kalman_filter(c(Nile, rep(NA, 10)), FF = 1, GG = 1, V = V_own, W = W_own,
                         m0 = 0, C0 = 1e7)
fc_check = dlmForecast(filt_check, nAhead = 10)

# Missing values (1910-1915 removed, as above):
kf_na         = kalman_filter(nile_na, FF = 1, GG = 1, V = V_own, W = W_own, m0 = 0, C0 = 1e7)
filt_na_check = dlmFilter(nile_na, mod_check)

diffs = c(
  max(abs(kf_nile$m[, 1] - as.numeric(filt_check$m))),
  max(abs(unlist(kf_nile$C) - unlist(dlmSvd2var(filt_check$U.C, filt_check$D.C)))),
  max(abs(ks_nile$s[, 1] - as.numeric(smooth_check$s))),
  max(abs(unlist(ks_nile$S) - unlist(dlmSvd2var(smooth_check$U.S, smooth_check$D.S)))),
  max(abs(kf_fc$f[101:110] - as.numeric(fc_check$f))),
  max(abs(kf_fc$Q[101:110] - unlist(fc_check$Q))),
  max(abs(kf_na$m[, 1] - as.numeric(filt_na_check$m))))

kable(data.frame(
  Check = c("Filtered means $m_t$",
            "Filtered variances $C_t$",
            "Smoothed means $s_t$",
            "Smoothed variances $S_t$",
            "Forecasts $f_{T+h}$, $h = 1, \\dots, 10$",
            "Forecast variances $Q_{T+h}$, $h = 1, \\dots, 10$",
            "Filtered means $m_t$ with missing values"),
  `Largest absolute difference` = formatC(diffs, format = "e", digits = 2),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE, align = "lr")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nile-loglik
#| tbl-cap: "Log-likelihood from my filter and from `dlmLL()`."

# dlmLL() returns -log L without the constant -(n/2) log(2*pi):
ll_dlm = -dlmLL(Nile, mod_check)

kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("$\\log L$ (own filter)",
               "$-\\texttt{dlmLL()}$",
               "Difference",
               "$-\\frac{n}{2}\\log(2\\pi)$"),
  Value = c(kf_nile$loglik, ll_dlm, kf_nile$loglik - ll_dlm,
            -length(Nile) / 2 * log(2 * pi))
), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE)
```

All differences in @tbl-nile-check are at the level of floating-point rounding error, so my filter and smoother reproduce `dlmFilter()`, `dlmSmooth()` and `dlmForecast()` to numerical precision, including the filtered means with missing values and the forecasts obtained by appending `NA`s. The two log-likelihoods in @tbl-nile-loglik differ only by the constant $-\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)$, which does not depend on the parameters, so both are maximised at the same values of $V$ and $W$.

The local level checks are all scalar, so they cannot detect matrix mistakes such as using $G_t' C_{t-1} G_t$ instead of $G_t C_{t-1} G_t'$. I therefore repeated the check for the local linear trend model, where $\theta_t = (\mu_t, \beta_t)'$ and $G = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is not symmetric, using the variances estimated earlier:

```{r}
G_llt = matrix(c(1, 0, 1, 1), 2, 2)   # [1 1; 0 1]

kf_llt = kalman_filter(Nile, FF = c(1, 0), GG = G_llt,
                       V = var_llt["V"], W = diag(var_llt[c("W_level", "W_slope")]),
                       m0 = c(0, 0), C0 = diag(1e7, 2))
filt_llt = dlmFilter(Nile, build_llt(fit_llt$par))

# Largest difference between own and dlm filtered states:
diff_llt = max(abs(kf_llt$m - filt_llt$m))
diff_llt
```

The largest difference in the filtered states is `r formatC(diff_llt, format = "e", digits = 1)`, so the matrix version of the filter also matches `dlmFilter()`.

## Topic exploration: exponential smoothing is a Kalman filter {#topic-exploration-exponential-smoothing-is-a-kalman-filter}

**Question:** *how is simple exponential smoothing related to the Kalman filter for the local level model?*

For the local level model ($F = G = 1$), the update step is

$$
m_t = m_{t-1} + K_t(y_t - m_{t-1}),
$$

which is exactly the error-correction form of SES, $\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha(y_t - \ell_{t-1})$, with a *time-varying* $\alpha = K_t$. The recursions for $R_t$, $C_t$ and $K_t$ do not involve $y_t$, so $K_t$ is a fixed sequence that can be computed before seeing any data, and for the local level model it converges to a steady state. Setting $C_t = C_{t-1} = C$ in $R_t = C_{t-1} + W$, $K_t = R_t/(R_t + V)$ and $C_t = (1 - K_t)R_t$ and solving gives

$$
K_\infty = \frac{-q + \sqrt{q^2 + 4q}}{2}, \qquad q = \frac{W}{V} \ (\text{the signal-to-noise ratio}).
$$

$K_\infty$ increases from 0 to 1 as $q$ increases. So, after a few observations, the Kalman filter for the local level model *is* SES with $\alpha = K_\infty$. The local level model also implies an ARIMA(0,1,1) for $y_t$ (with $\theta = K_\infty - 1 \in (-1, 0)$), and the ARIMA(0,1,1) forecast is SES with $\alpha = 1 + \theta$. @tbl-kalman-gain compares the steady-state gain with the gain from my filter, the ARIMA(0,1,1) estimate and the `ses()` estimate for the Nile data:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-kalman-gain
#| tbl-cap: "Steady-state Kalman gain, the ARIMA(0,1,1) estimate and the SES smoothing parameter for the Nile data."

q_nile = W_own / V_own
K_inf = (-q_nile + sqrt(q_nile^2 + 4 * q_nile)) / 2

# Kalman gain at each time point from own filter (F = 1, so K_t = R_t / Q_t):
K_t = unlist(kf_nile$R) / kf_nile$Q

# SES and ARIMA(0,1,1) fitted to the same data:
ses_nile = ses(Nile)
arima_nile = Arima(Nile, order = c(0, 1, 1))

kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Steady-state Kalman gain $K_\\infty$ (from $\\hat{V}$ and $\\hat{W}$)",
               "Kalman gain $K_{100}$ from my filter",
               "$1 + \\hat{\\theta}$ from ARIMA(0,1,1)",
               "$\\hat{\\alpha}$ from `ses()`"),
  Value = c(K_inf, K_t[100], 1 + coef(arima_nile)["ma1"], ses_nile$model$par["alpha"])
), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-kalman-gain
#| fig-cap: "Kalman gain $K_t$ of the local level model for the Nile data (pink), converging to its steady state $K_\\infty$ (purple dashed). The grey dotted line is the smoothing parameter estimated by `ses()`."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

ggplot(data = data.frame(t = 1:30, K = K_t[1:30]), mapping = aes(x = t, y = K)) +
  geom_line(col = "deeppink") +
  geom_point(col = "deeppink") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = K_inf, linetype = 2, col = "purple") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = ses_nile$model$par["alpha"], linetype = 3, col = "grey40") +
  labs(title = "Kalman gain for the Nile local level model.", x = "Time", y = expression(K[t])) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The Kalman gain starts close to 1 (the vague prior means the first observation gets almost all the weight) and settles at $K_\infty \approx `r round(K_inf, 3)`$ within about ten years (@fig-kalman-gain). $1 + \hat{\theta} = `r round(1 + coef(arima_nile)["ma1"], 3)`$ from the ARIMA(0,1,1) is almost identical, because the local level model is an ARIMA(0,1,1) with $\theta$ restricted to $(-1, 0)$, and both are fitted by maximum likelihood. The SES estimate is close but smaller ($\hat{\alpha} = `r round(ses_nile[["model"]][["par"]]["alpha"], 3)`$). The difference comes from how the parameters are estimated: `ses()` fits the single-source-of-error model ETS(A,N,N) and estimates $\ell_0$ as a parameter, while the local level model has two independent errors and a vague prior on the initial level. With the same $\alpha$ the three approaches would give identical forecasts once the filter has reached its steady state. With the estimated values the forecasts differ only slightly.

This gives the smoothing parameter $\alpha$ a clear meaning: it is determined by the signal-to-noise ratio $q = W/V$. A noisy series with a slowly moving level (small $q$, like the Nile) gives a small $\alpha$, so the forecast averages over many years. A series whose level moves a lot compared to the noise (like the oil data in Question 2) gives $\alpha$ close to 1, so the forecast is essentially the last observation.

## Tutorial: State-space models and the Kalman filter

### Question 1: Simulation and a Kalman filter from first principles

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= F_t\theta_t + v_t, \qquad v_t \sim N(0, V = 2) \\
\theta_t &= G_t\theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad w_t \sim N(0, W = 1) \\
\theta_0 &\sim N(0, 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

with $G_t = \frac{1}{2}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}[2t+1]\right) = \frac{(-1)^t}{2}$ (since $\sin(\pi t + \pi/2) = \cos(\pi t) = (-1)^t$), and $F_t \sim N(1, 0.2^2)$ rounded to one decimal, playing the role of an explanatory variable.

Because $G_t$ alternates in sign, half of the previous state carries over with a flipped sign every step. This creates the cyclical (zig-zag) behaviour in $\theta_t$.

```{r}
set.seed(42)

n_kf = 100
h_kf = 5
N_kf = n_kf + h_kf
V_true = 2
W_true = 1

# Time-varying system matrices (F_t also needed for forecast period):
FF_t = round(rnorm(N_kf, 1, 0.2), 1)
GG_t = (-1)^(1:N_kf) / 2

# Simulate the states and observations:
theta_kf = numeric(N_kf)
y_kf = numeric(N_kf)
theta_prev = rnorm(1, 0, 1)                                     # theta_0
for (t in 1:N_kf) {
  theta_kf[t] = GG_t[t] * theta_prev + rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(W_true)) # state equation
  y_kf[t] = FF_t[t] * theta_kf[t] + rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(V_true))    # observation equation
  theta_prev = theta_kf[t]
}

# Observed series (last 5 values held out to check forecasts):
y_obs = c(y_kf[1:n_kf], rep(NA, h_kf))
```

#### Parameter estimation

I use my `kalman_filter()` from above, with $F_t$ and $G_t$ passed as functions of $t$. The likelihood is maximised over $\log V$ and $\log W$. The 5 `NA`s at the end do not contribute to the likelihood.

```{r}
# Function to calculate negative log-likelihood from log variances:
negll = function(parm, y, FF, GG) {
  -kalman_filter(y, FF = function(t) FF[t], GG = function(t) GG[t],
                 V = exp(parm[1]), W = exp(parm[2]), m0 = 0, C0 = 1)$loglik
}

fit_kf = optim(par = c(0, 0), fn = negll, y = y_obs, FF = FF_t, GG = GG_t,
               method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)

se_kf = sqrt(diag(solve(fit_kf$hessian)))
kable(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("V", "W"),
  True = c(V_true, W_true),
  Estimate = exp(fit_kf$par),
  Lower = exp(fit_kf$par - 1.96 * se_kf),
  Upper = exp(fit_kf$par + 1.96 * se_kf)
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

V_hat = exp(fit_kf$par[1])
W_hat = exp(fit_kf$par[2])
kf_out = kalman_filter(y_obs, FF = function(t) FF_t[t], GG = function(t) GG_t[t],
                       V = V_hat, W = W_hat, m0 = 0, C0 = 1)

# Filtered states and variances (without time-0 row):
m_kf = kf_out$m[-1, 1]
C_kf = unlist(kf_out$C[-1])
```

Both true values lie inside their 95% intervals ($\hat{V} = `r round(V_hat, 2)`$ and $\hat{W} = `r round(W_hat, 2)`$), but the intervals are wide, especially for $W$, whose upper limit is more than ten times its lower limit. The two variances are not easy to separate. Since $|G_t| = 1/2$, the state forgets its past quickly, so $\theta_t$ is close to white noise and $y_t$ looks like noise with variance $F_t^2\,\text{Var}(\theta_t) + V$. The changing $F_t$ helps a little, because it scales the state part but not the observation noise, but the confidence intervals are still wide.

**Check against `dlm`.** `dlm` allows time-varying matrices through `JFF`, `JGG` and `X`: the entries of `JFF`/`JGG` say which column of `X` holds the value at each time.

```{r}
mod_tv = dlm(FF = matrix(1), V = matrix(V_hat), GG = matrix(1), W = matrix(W_hat),
             m0 = 0, C0 = matrix(1),
             JFF = matrix(1), JGG = matrix(2), X = cbind(FF_t, GG_t))
filt_tv = dlmFilter(y_obs, mod_tv)

# Largest difference between own and dlm filtered states:
max(abs(as.numeric(dropFirst(filt_tv$m)) - m_kf))
```

My Kalman filter gives the same filtered states as `dlmFilter()`, including the 5 missing values at the end.

#### Forecasts for $h = 1, \ldots, 5$

Adding `NA`s to the end of $y$ makes the filter skip the update step, so $m_t = a_t$, $C_t = R_t$, and $f_t, Q_t$ are the forecasts and their variances.

```{r}
fc_idx = (n_kf + 1):N_kf
kable(data.frame(
  h = 1:h_kf,
  Forecast = kf_out$f[fc_idx],
  Lower = kf_out$f[fc_idx] - 1.96 * sqrt(kf_out$Q[fc_idx]),
  Upper = kf_out$f[fc_idx] + 1.96 * sqrt(kf_out$Q[fc_idx]),
  True_y = y_kf[fc_idx]
), digits = 2, escape = FALSE,
col.names = c("$h$", "Forecast", "Lower", "Upper", "True $y_{100+h}$"))
```

The forecasts shrink towards zero almost immediately: after one step only half of the last state survives (with a sign flip), after two steps a quarter, and so on. The prediction intervals quickly reach their long-run width, $\pm 1.96\sqrt{F_t^2 \text{Var}(\theta) + V}$ with $\text{Var}(\theta) = W/(1 - 1/4)$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-kf-fit
#| fig-cap: "Kalman filter results for the simulated model in Question 1."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Observations (grey), one-step-ahead fitted values (pink) and filtered signal $F_t m_t$ (blue), with forecasts and 95% prediction intervals for $t = 101, \\ldots, 105$."
#|   - "True state $\\theta_t$ (black) and filtered state $m_t$ with 95% interval (pink)."
#| layout-nrow: 2
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

kf_df = data.frame(
  t = 1:N_kf,
  y = y_kf,
  observed = c(rep(TRUE, n_kf), rep(FALSE, h_kf)),
  f = kf_out$f,
  f_lo = kf_out$f - 1.96 * sqrt(kf_out$Q),
  f_hi = kf_out$f + 1.96 * sqrt(kf_out$Q),
  signal = FF_t * m_kf,
  theta = theta_kf,
  m = m_kf,
  m_lo = m_kf - 1.96 * sqrt(C_kf),
  m_hi = m_kf + 1.96 * sqrt(C_kf)
)

p_top = ggplot(data = kf_df, mapping = aes(x = t)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = kf_df[!kf_df$observed, ], aes(ymin = f_lo, ymax = f_hi),
              fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(y = y, shape = observed), col = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(y = f), col = "deeppink") +
  geom_line(data = kf_df[kf_df$observed, ], aes(y = signal), col = "steelblue") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("TRUE" = 16, "FALSE" = 4),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "Used for fitting", "FALSE" = "Held out")) +
  labs(title = "Observations, fitted values and forecasts.", x = "Time", y = "y", shape = "") +
  theme_minimal()

p_bottom = ggplot(data = kf_df, mapping = aes(x = t)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = m_lo, ymax = m_hi), fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theta), col = "black") +
  geom_line(aes(y = m), col = "deeppink") +
  labs(title = "True and filtered state.", x = "Time", y = expression(theta[t])) +
  theme_minimal()

print(p_top)
print(p_bottom)
```

#### Residuals

```{r}
#| label: fig-kf-res
#| fig-cap: "Standardised one-step-ahead prediction errors from my Kalman filter and their ACF."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

std_res = kf_out$e[1:n_kf] / sqrt(kf_out$Q[1:n_kf])

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(std_res, type = "h", col = "deeppink", xlab = "Time", ylab = "Standardised residual",
     main = "Standardised residuals")
abline(h = 0)
acf(std_res, main = "ACF")
```

```{r}
lb_kf = Box.test(std_res, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 2)
lb_kf
```

The standardised prediction errors $e_t/\sqrt{Q_t}$ should be independent $N(0,1)$ if the model is correct, which it is here (we simulated from it). The ACF (@fig-kf-res) and the Ljung--Box test ($p = `r round(lb_kf[["p.value"]], 3)`$) are consistent with this.

**Discussion.** The filtered state follows the zig-zag pattern of the true state, but with wide intervals: with $V = 2$ and a state variance of only about $1.33$, a single observation carries limited information about $\theta_t$ (@fig-kf-fit). The filter gives the most weight to the observation when $F_t$ is large, because then the state part of $y_t$ is larger relative to the noise.

### Question 2: A noisy AR(2) process

$$
x_t = -0.9x_{t-2} + w_t, \qquad y_t = x_t + v_t.
$$

#### a) State-space form

Let $\theta_t = (x_t, x_{t-1})'$. Then

$$
\theta_t = \begin{pmatrix} x_t \\ x_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}
= \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -0.9 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{G}
\begin{pmatrix} x_{t-1} \\ x_{t-2} \end{pmatrix} +
\begin{pmatrix} w_t \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
W = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2_w & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
$$

$$
y_t = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{F}\theta_t + v_t, \qquad V = \sigma^2_v,
\qquad \theta_0 = (x_0, x_{-1})'.
$$

#### b) Initial variances for stationarity

$x_t$ only depends on $x_{t-2}$, so the even and odd time points form two independent AR(1) processes (in steps of two) with coefficient $-0.9$. For $x_t$ (and hence $y_t$) to be stationary from the start, $x_0$ and $x_{-1}$ must come from the stationary distribution:

$$
\sigma^2_0 = \sigma^2_1 = \frac{\sigma^2_w}{1 - 0.9^2} = \frac{\sigma^2_w}{0.19},
$$

and $x_0$ and $x_{-1}$ are uncorrelated, since $\text{Cov}(x_t, x_{t-1}) = 0$ for this process. With $\sigma_w = 1$ this gives $\sigma^2_0 = \sigma^2_1 = `r round(1 / 0.19, 3)`$. Then $\text{Var}(y_t) = \sigma^2_w/0.19 + \sigma^2_v$ for every $t$.

#### c) and d) Simulation with $\sigma_v = 1$ and $\sigma_v = 10$

```{r}
# Simulate x and y:
sim_q2 = function(n, sigma_w, sigma_v) {
  s2_0 = sigma_w^2 / (1 - 0.9^2)              # stationary variance
  x_all = numeric(n + 2)
  x_all[1:2] = rnorm(2, 0, sqrt(s2_0))        # x_{-1}, x_0
  for (t in 3:(n + 2)) {
    x_all[t] = -0.9 * x_all[t - 2] + rnorm(1, 0, sigma_w)
  }
  x = x_all[-(1:2)]
  y = x + rnorm(n, 0, sigma_v)                # observation noise
  return(list(x = ts(x), y = ts(y)))
}

# Same seed so both cases share the same x:
set.seed(8)
q2_v1 = sim_q2(100, sigma_w = 1, sigma_v = 1)
set.seed(8)
q2_v10 = sim_q2(100, sigma_w = 1, sigma_v = 10)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-q2-time
#| fig-cap: "The AR(2) state process $x_t$ (pink) and the noisy observations $y_t$ (grey) for $\\sigma_v = 1$ (left) and $\\sigma_v = 10$ (right)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(q2_v1$y, col = "grey50", ylab = "", main = expression(sigma[v] == 1))
lines(q2_v1$x, col = "deeppink", lwd = 2)
plot(q2_v10$y, col = "grey50", ylab = "", main = expression(sigma[v] == 10))
lines(q2_v10$x, col = "deeppink", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-q2-acf
#| fig-cap: "Sample ACF and PACF of $x_t$ and $y_t$. Rows: $x_t$, $y_t$ with $\\sigma_v = 1$, and $y_t$ with $\\sigma_v = 10$."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

par(mfrow = c(3, 2))
acf(q2_v1$x, main = "ACF of x", lag.max = 20)
pacf(q2_v1$x, main = "PACF of x", lag.max = 20)
acf(q2_v1$y, main = "ACF of y (sigma_v = 1)", lag.max = 20)
pacf(q2_v1$y, main = "PACF of y (sigma_v = 1)", lag.max = 20)
acf(q2_v10$y, main = "ACF of y (sigma_v = 10)", lag.max = 20)
pacf(q2_v10$y, main = "PACF of y (sigma_v = 10)", lag.max = 20)
```

```{r}
# Theoretical ACF of x:
round(ARMAacf(ar = c(0, -0.9), lag.max = 8), 3)

# Factor by which observation noise shrinks autocorrelations of y:
var_x = 1 / 0.19
c(sigma_v_1 = var_x / (var_x + 1), sigma_v_10 = var_x / (var_x + 100))
```

-   $x_t$: the theoretical ACF is zero at odd lags and $(-0.9)^{k}$ at lag $2k$, so it alternates in sign at even lags and decays slowly. The PACF has a single large spike of about $-0.9$ at lag 2, as expected for an AR(2) with $\phi_1 = 0$. The time plot (@fig-q2-time) shows a regular cycle with a period of about 4 time steps.
-   $y_t$ with $\sigma_v = 1$: the autocorrelations of $y$ are those of $x$ multiplied by $\text{Var}(x)/(\text{Var}(x) + \sigma^2_v) = `r round(var_x / (var_x + 1), 2)`$, so the pattern is still clearly visible. The PACF no longer cuts off exactly after lag 2: adding white noise to an AR(2) gives an ARMA(2, 2), so smaller partial autocorrelations appear at later lags.
-   $y_t$ with $\sigma_v = 10$: the shrinkage factor is only `r round(var_x / (var_x + 100), 2)`. The signal is buried in the noise: the ACF and PACF of $y$ look like white noise even though $x$ is strongly autocorrelated (@fig-q2-acf).

This is exactly the situation where a state-space model helps: we model $x$ directly and treat $v$ as measurement error. As an extra check I ran my Kalman filter and smoother with the true parameters to recover $x$ from $y$:

```{r}
G_q2 = matrix(c(0, 1, -0.9, 0), 2, 2)   # [0 -0.9; 1 0]

# Function to compute smoothed estimate of x_t (first state) with own filter and smoother:
smooth_x = function(y, sigma_v) {
  kf = kalman_filter(as.numeric(y), FF = c(1, 0), GG = G_q2, V = sigma_v^2,
                     W = diag(c(1, 0)), m0 = c(0, 0), C0 = diag(1 / 0.19, 2))
  kalman_smoother(kf, GG = G_q2)$s[-1, 1]
}
x_hat_v1 = smooth_x(q2_v1$y, sigma_v = 1)
x_hat_v10 = smooth_x(q2_v10$y, sigma_v = 10)

# Correlation between true x and its smoothed estimate:
c(sigma_v_1 = cor(q2_v1$x, x_hat_v1), sigma_v_10 = cor(q2_v10$x, x_hat_v10))
```

With $\sigma_v = 1$ the smoothed estimate of $x$ is very close to the truth (correlation `r round(cor(q2_v1$x, x_hat_v1), 2)`). With $\sigma_v = 10$ the correlation drops to `r round(cor(q2_v10$x, x_hat_v10), 2)`, which is still surprisingly high given that the ACF and PACF of $y$ looked like white noise. The smoother can recover so much because it is given the true model. It knows that $x$ follows a strong cycle with period 4, so it can average over many noisy observations that carry information about the same cycle. In practice the parameters would have to be estimated, and with this much noise that would be challenging

### Question 3: Second differences of the linear growth model

The linear growth model is

$$
Y_t = \mu_t + v_t, \qquad \mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad \beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + \gamma_t,
$$

with $v_t$, $w_t$, $\gamma_t$ independent white noise with variances $\sigma^2_v, \sigma^2_w, \sigma^2_\gamma$.

**First difference of the level:** $\Delta\mu_t = \mu_t - \mu_{t-1} = \beta_{t-1} + w_t$.

**Second difference of the level:** $\Delta^2\mu_t = (\beta_{t-1} - \beta_{t-2}) + (w_t - w_{t-1}) = \gamma_{t-1} + w_t - w_{t-1}$.

**Second difference of the noise:** $\Delta^2 v_t = v_t - 2v_{t-1} + v_{t-2}$.

So

$$
Z_t = \Delta^2 Y_t = \gamma_{t-1} + w_t - w_{t-1} + v_t - 2v_{t-1} + v_{t-2}.
$$

$Z_t$ is a finite linear combination of white noise terms at lags 0, 1 and 2, so its mean (0) and autocovariances do not depend on $t$ (it is stationary). Using the independence of all the noise terms, the autocovariances are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_Z(0) &= \sigma^2_\gamma + 2\sigma^2_w + (1 + 4 + 1)\sigma^2_v = \sigma^2_\gamma + 2\sigma^2_w + 6\sigma^2_v \\
\gamma_Z(1) &= \text{Cov}(Z_t, Z_{t-1}) = -\sigma^2_w + (-2)(1)\sigma^2_v + (1)(-2)\sigma^2_v = -\sigma^2_w - 4\sigma^2_v \\
\gamma_Z(2) &= \text{Cov}(Z_t, Z_{t-2}) = (1)(1)\sigma^2_v = \sigma^2_v \\
\gamma_Z(k) &= 0, \quad k \geq 3
\end{aligned}
$$

An autocovariance function that is non-zero up to lag 2 and zero afterwards is exactly the ACF of an MA(2) process. (Any stationary process whose autocovariances cut off after lag $q$ can be written as an MA($q$).) So the linear growth model is an ARIMA(0,2,2) model.

**Simulation check:**

```{r}
set.seed(9)
n_lg = 10000
sig_v = 1
sig_w = 0.5
sig_g = 0.2

# Simulate the linear growth model:
beta_lg = cumsum(rnorm(n_lg, 0, sig_g))
mu_lg = numeric(n_lg)
for (t in 2:n_lg) mu_lg[t] = mu_lg[t - 1] + beta_lg[t - 1] + rnorm(1, 0, sig_w)
y_lg = mu_lg + rnorm(n_lg, 0, sig_v)

# Second differences:
z_lg = diff(y_lg, differences = 2)

# Theoretical ACF:
g0 = sig_g^2 + 2 * sig_w^2 + 6 * sig_v^2
rho_theory = c(1, (-sig_w^2 - 4 * sig_v^2) / g0, sig_v^2 / g0, 0, 0)

# Sample ACF and ACF of fitted MA(2):
ma2 = arima(z_lg, order = c(0, 0, 2), include.mean = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Lag = 0:4,
  Theory = rho_theory,
  Sample = as.numeric(acf(z_lg, lag.max = 4, plot = FALSE)$acf),
  Fitted_MA2 = as.numeric(ARMAacf(ma = coef(ma2), lag.max = 4))
), digits = 3, col.names = c("Lag", "Theory", "Sample", "Fitted MA(2)"))
```

The sample ACF of the second differences matches the theoretical values, and is zero beyond lag 2. A fitted MA(2) reproduces the same ACF.

### Question 4: Regression coefficients with a Kalman filter

The tutorial uses `usconsumption` from the (older) `fpp` package. The same quarterly growth rates for US personal consumption and disposable income are in `uschange` in `fpp2` (with more recent data, 1970--2016), so I used those.

```{r}
# Read in data:
data(uschange)
# View(uschange)

y_us = uschange[, "Consumption"]
z_us = uschange[, "Income"]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-us-data
#| fig-cap: "Quarterly percentage changes in US consumption and income (left) and consumption against income with the least squares line (right)."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Time plot"
#|   - "Scatter plot"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

us_df = data.frame(
  quarter = rep(as.numeric(time(y_us)), 2),
  change = c(as.numeric(y_us), as.numeric(z_us)),
  series = rep(c("Consumption", "Income"), each = length(y_us))
)

ggplot(data = us_df, mapping = aes(x = quarter, y = change, colour = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Consumption" = "deeppink", "Income" = "grey50")) +
  labs(title = "US quarterly growth rates.", x = "Quarter", y = "% change", colour = "") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggplot(data = data.frame(income = as.numeric(z_us), consumption = as.numeric(y_us)),
       mapping = aes(x = income, y = consumption)) +
  geom_point(col = "deeppink") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = "black") +
  labs(title = "Consumption vs income.", x = "Income (% change)", y = "Consumption (% change)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

@fig-us-data shows that consumption and income growth move together, but income growth is much more volatile, and the scatter plot shows a positive but noisy relationship.

```{r}
# Ordinary least squares:
lm_us = lm(y_us ~ z_us)
summary(lm_us)$coefficients
```

#### The Kalman filter for regression

As a state-space model, $\theta_t = (a_t, b_t)'$, $G = I$, $W = 0$ (the coefficients do not change), $F_t = (1, z_t)$ and $V = \sigma^2$. This is my `kalman_filter()` with $F_t$ given as a function of $t$:

```{r}
n_us = length(y_us)
z_vec = as.numeric(z_us)

kf_reg = function(sigma2) {
  kalman_filter(as.numeric(y_us), FF = function(t) c(1, z_vec[t]), GG = diag(2),
                V = sigma2, W = matrix(0, 2, 2), m0 = c(0, 0), C0 = diag(1e7, 2))
}

kf_us_1 = kf_reg(sigma2 = 1)
kf_us_100 = kf_reg(sigma2 = 100)

# Filtered coefficients and diagonal of C_t (without time-0 row):
coef_path = kf_us_1$m[-1, ]
C_diag = t(sapply(kf_us_1$C[-1], diag))

kable(data.frame(
  Coefficient = c("a (intercept)", "b (slope)"),
  OLS = coef(lm_us),
  KF_sigma2_1 = kf_us_1$m[n_us + 1, ],
  KF_sigma2_100 = kf_us_100$m[n_us + 1, ]
), digits = 5, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE,
col.names = c("Coefficient", "OLS", "Kalman filter ($\\sigma^2 = 1$)", "Kalman filter ($\\sigma^2 = 100$)"))
```

The final filtered estimates $m_T$ are identical to the OLS estimates (up to the effect of the very vague prior), whatever value of $\sigma^2$ is used.

::: callout-note
## Why $\sigma^2$ does not matter

With $W = 0$ and a prior variance proportional to $\sigma^2$ ($C_0 = \sigma^2 C_0^*$), every variance in the filter ($R_t$, $C_t$ and $Q_t$) is proportional to $\sigma^2$. The Kalman gain $K_t = R_tF_t'/Q_t$ is a ratio of these, so $\sigma^2$ cancels and the filtered means $m_t$ do not depend on it. Only the variances $C_t$ do. Here $C_0 = 10^7 I$ is fixed rather than scaled by $\sigma^2$, but it is so vague that its effect on $m_t$ is negligible for both $\sigma^2 = 1$ and $\sigma^2 = 100$.
:::

#### Estimating $\sigma^2$

Run the filter with $\sigma^2 = 1$. The standardised prediction errors $e_t/\sqrt{Q_t}$ then have variance $\sigma^2$. The first two have (almost) zero weight because the prior is vague and two coefficients have to be learned first, so

$$
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{T-2}\sum_{t=3}^{T} \frac{e_t^2}{Q_t}.
$$

```{r}
sigma2_kf = sum(kf_us_1$e[-(1:2)]^2 / kf_us_1$Q[-(1:2)]) / (n_us - 2)
c(kalman_filter = sigma2_kf, lm = summary(lm_us)$sigma^2)
```

These are the same: the sum of squared standardised one-step-ahead errors (the *recursive residuals*) equals the OLS residual sum of squares.

#### Recursive coefficient estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-us-recursive
#| fig-cap: "Recursive (filtered) estimates of the intercept and slope, with approximate 95% intervals, from quarter 10 onwards. Dashed lines: full-sample OLS estimates."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

rec_df = data.frame(
  quarter = rep(as.numeric(time(y_us)), 2),
  coef = rep(c("Intercept (a)", "Slope (b)"), each = n_us),
  est = c(coef_path[, 1], coef_path[, 2]),
  se = sqrt(c(C_diag[, 1], C_diag[, 2]) * sigma2_kf),
  ols = rep(coef(lm_us), each = n_us)
)
rec_df = rec_df[rep(1:n_us, 2) >= 10, ]

ggplot(data = rec_df, mapping = aes(x = quarter, y = est)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = est - 1.96 * se, ymax = est + 1.96 * se), fill = "deeppink", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(col = "deeppink") +
  geom_line(aes(y = ols), linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~coef, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Recursive regression estimates.",
    x = "Quarter",
    y = "Estimate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

$m_t$ is (up to the vague prior) the OLS estimate using only the data up to quarter $t$ (@fig-us-recursive). If the relationship were constant, these estimates should settle down and then only fluctuate within their intervals. Systematic drift (for example a slope that keeps decreasing) suggests that the coefficients change over time.

Here the estimates do not settle down smoothly. After the noisy start, the slope stays around 0.4 to 0.5 until the early 1980s and then drifts down to the full-sample value of about 0.28, with sudden jumps around 1980, 2001 and 2013. Even after 100 or more quarters a single quarter can move the recursive slope noticeably, which suggests that a few quarters with unusually large income changes are influential, or that the relationship has changed over time.

Recursive estimates are a weak test, though, because every new estimate still uses all the earlier data. A more direct approach is to let the coefficients follow random walks ($W > 0$) and compare the likelihoods.

```{r}
#| warning: false

# Static (W = 0) vs time-varying (W estimated) coefficients:
build_static = function(p) dlmModReg(z_us, dV = exp(p[1]), dW = c(0, 0))
build_tvp = function(p) dlmModReg(z_us, dV = exp(p[1]), dW = exp(p[2:3]))

fit_static = dlmMLE(y_us, parm = log(var(y_us)), build = build_static, method = "BFGS")
fit_tvp = dlmMLE(y_us, parm = c(log(var(y_us)), -5, -5), build = build_tvp)

kable(data.frame(
  Model = c("Static coefficients", "Time-varying coefficients"),
  Parameters = c(1, 3),
  neg_loglik = c(fit_static$value, fit_tvp$value),
  AIC = c(2 * fit_static$value + 2 * 1, 2 * fit_tvp$value + 2 * 3)
), digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE,
col.names = c("Model", "Parameters", "$-\\log L$", "AIC"))

signif(exp(fit_tvp$par), 3)  # V, W_a, W_b
```

The time-varying coefficient model has a much lower AIC (`r round(2 * fit_tvp$value + 6, 1)` vs `r round(2 * fit_static$value + 2, 1)`), and neither coefficient variance is close to zero ($\hat{W}_a = `r signif(exp(fit_tvp[["par"]][2]), 2)`$, $\hat{W}_b =`r signif(exp(fit_tvp[["par"]][3]), 2)`$). The observation variance drops from about `r round(exp(fit_static$par), 2)` to `r round(exp(fit_tvp$par[1]), 2)`. So the data favour coefficients that change over time. (Because $W = 0$ lies on the boundary of the parameter space, the usual $\chi^2$ reference distribution for a likelihood ratio test does not apply, but the AIC difference is large enough for this not to matter.) The smoothed coefficients (@fig-us-tvp) show how the relationship evolved. The slope is highest (about 0.5 to 0.6) in the 1970s and falls to around 0.1 after 2000, so consumption growth has become less sensitive to income growth. The intercept moves a lot and drops sharply in the 2008--2009 recession, so the random-walk intercept also picks up slow movements in consumption growth that income does not explain:

```{r}
#| label: fig-us-tvp
#| fig-cap: "Smoothed coefficients from the time-varying coefficient model."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

smooth_tvp = dlmSmooth(y_us, build_tvp(fit_tvp$par))
tvp_df = data.frame(
  quarter = rep(as.numeric(time(y_us)), 2),
  coef = rep(c("Intercept (a)", "Slope (b)"), each = n_us),
  est = c(dropFirst(smooth_tvp$s)[, 1], dropFirst(smooth_tvp$s)[, 2])
)

ggplot(data = tvp_df, mapping = aes(x = quarter, y = est)) +
  geom_line(col = "deeppink") +
  facet_wrap(~coef, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Time-varying regression coefficients.", x = "Quarter", y = "Estimate") +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### The same filter with `dlm`

```{r}
mod_us = dlmModReg(z_us, dV = 1, dW = c(0, 0))  # default prior: m0 = 0, C0 = 1e7 I
filt_us = dlmFilter(y_us, mod_us)

# Largest difference between own and dlm filtered coefficients:
max(abs(filt_us$m[-1, ] - coef_path))
```

`dlmModReg()` uses the same vague prior, so `dlmFilter()` gives the same sequence of coefficient estimates as my own filter.

# Hidden Markov Models {#hidden-markov-models}

This section works through Questions 1 to 7 of the HMM tutorial. It uses the HMM toolkit (scaled forward and backward algorithms, local decoding, the Viterbi algorithm and the stationary distribution) that I wrote from first principles for [Project 4](../projects/project-04-analysis.qmd), where the toolkit is explained in detail. Question 8, Poisson HMMs for the earthquake counts, is in Project 4, because it is where I checked the toolkit against `depmixS4` before applying it to JSE returns.

```{r}
#| label: hmm-setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)

# Same seed and colours as in Project 4:
set.seed(2026)
col_main   = "purple"
col_accent = "deeppink"
state_cols = c("1" = "steelblue", "2" = "purple", "3" = "deeppink", "4" = "black")
```

```{r}
#| label: hmm-toolkit
#| file: ../scripts/hmm-toolkit.R
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "HMM toolkit (scripts/hmm-toolkit.R)"
```

## Question 1: Simulating a three-state bivariate Gaussian HMM

```{r}
#| label: q1-sim

# State-dependent means and covariance matrices (sigma must be created first):
mu_q1 = 10 * matrix(c(-1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
sf = 10    # scaling factor
sigma_q1 = array(NA, dim = c(2, 2, 3))
sigma_q1[, , 1] = sf * matrix(c(1, 1/2, 1/2, 1), nrow = 2)
sigma_q1[, , 2] = sf * matrix(c(1, -1/2, -1/2, 1), nrow = 2)
sigma_q1[, , 3] = sf * matrix(c(3, 0, 0, 1/2), nrow = 2)

Gamma_q1 = matrix(c(0.8, 0.1, 0.1,
                    0.1, 0.8, 0.1,
                    0.1, 0.1, 0.8), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# Simulate 20 observations (Gamma symmetric, so stationary dist is uniform):
n_q1 = 20
z_q1 = numeric(n_q1)
x_q1 = matrix(NA, n_q1, 2)
for (t in 1:n_q1) {
  z_q1[t] = if (t == 1) sample(1:3, 1) else sample(1:3, 1, prob = Gamma_q1[z_q1[t - 1], ])
  x_q1[t, ] = MASS::mvrnorm(1, mu = mu_q1[z_q1[t], ], Sigma = sigma_q1[, , z_q1[t]])
}

q1_df = tibble(t = 1:n_q1, x1 = x_q1[, 1], x2 = x_q1[, 2], state = factor(z_q1))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-q1
#| fig-cap: "Twenty observations simulated from the three-state bivariate Gaussian HMM, coloured by the true state. The grey arrows show the time path and the crosses mark the state means."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

ggplot(data = q1_df, mapping = aes(x = x1, y = x2)) +
  geom_path(col = "grey70", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = state), size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = t), nudge_y = 0.9, size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = tibble(x1 = mu_q1[, 1], x2 = mu_q1[, 2]), shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = state_cols) +
  labs(title = "Simulated three-state Gaussian HMM.", x = expression(x[1]), y = expression(x[2]),
       colour = "State") +
  theme_minimal()
```

@fig-q1 shows the three state distributions: state 1 is centred at $(-10, 0)$ with positive correlation, state 2 at $(10, 0)$ with negative correlation and state 3 at $(0, 10)$ with a much larger variance in $x_1$ than in $x_2$. Because the diagonal of $\Gamma$ is 0.8, the process stays in a state for five steps on average ($1/(1-0.8)$), so consecutive points tend to come from the same cluster, and the path jumps between clusters only occasionally.

Given only the observations, we would need:

-   the transition probabilities: $3 \times 2 = 6$,
-   the state means: $3 \times 2 = 6$,
-   the covariance matrices: $3 \times 3 = 9$,
-   the initial distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}$: 2 more.

That is 21 parameters (23 with $\boldsymbol{\delta}$), estimated from 20 bivariate observations (40 numbers). With so few observations the estimates would be very unreliable, and some states might not be visited often enough to estimate their covariance matrices at all.

## Question 2: The Viterbi algorithm by hand

```{r}
#| label: q2

obs_q2  = c("x", "x", "x", "x", "x", "x", "x", "z", "z", "y")
true_q2 = c("A", "C", "A", "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B")

init = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3)
tpm = matrix(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0.6, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2, 0.6), byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3)
emmprob = matrix(c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.3, 0.4), byrow = TRUE, ncol = 3)
colnames(emmprob) = c("x", "y", "z")   # observations along columns
state_names = c("A", "B", "C")

# Emission probabilities for observed words (dens[t, i] = P(x_t | C_t = i)):
dens_q2 = t(emmprob[, obs_q2])

vit_q2 = hmm_viterbi(dens_q2, init, tpm)
local_q2 = hmm_local(dens_q2, init, tpm)

q2_tbl = tibble(t = 1:10,
                Observation = obs_q2,
                `xi(A)` = vit_q2$xi[, 1], `xi(B)` = vit_q2$xi[, 2], `xi(C)` = vit_q2$xi[, 3],
                Viterbi = state_names[vit_q2$states],
                `P(A | x)` = local_q2[, 1], `P(B | x)` = local_q2[, 2], `P(C | x)` = local_q2[, 3],
                `True state` = true_q2)

kable(q2_tbl, digits = 3, escape = FALSE,
      col.names = c("$t$", "Observation", "$\\xi_{tA}$", "$\\xi_{tB}$", "$\\xi_{tC}$", "Viterbi",
                    "$P(C_t = A \\mid \\mathbf{x})$", "$P(C_t = B \\mid \\mathbf{x})$",
                    "$P(C_t = C \\mid \\mathbf{x})$", "True state"))
```

The Viterbi algorithm fills in $\xi_{ti}$, the log-probability of the most likely path that ends in state $i$ at time $t$ (together with the observations up to $t$):

$$
\xi_{1i} = \log\delta_i + \log p_i(x_1), \qquad \xi_{tj} = \max_i\left(\xi_{t-1,i} + \log\gamma_{ij}\right) + \log p_j(x_t).
$$

The most likely final state is the one with the largest $\xi_{Ti}$, and the path is traced back with $S_t = \text{argmax}_i(\xi_{ti} + \log\gamma_{i,S_{t+1}})$. Working on the log scale turns the products into sums and avoids underflow.

The most likely state sequence is **`r paste(state_names[vit_q2$states], collapse = "")`**, which agrees with the true sequence at `r sum(state_names[vit_q2$states] == true_q2)` of the 10 time points. The first seven observations are all "x", which state A emits with probability 0.6 (compared with 0.1 and 0.3 for B and C). A is the least persistent state ($\gamma_{AA} = 0.5$), but the emission probabilities outweigh this, so the algorithm stays in A. At time 8 the path switches to B. "z" is equally likely in B and C (0.4), and B and C are equally persistent ($\gamma_{BB} = \gamma_{CC} = 0.6$), but A moves to B more often than to C (0.3 vs 0.2) and the final "y" is more likely in B (0.5 vs 0.3).

The only mistake is at time 2, where the true state is C. A single "x" from C between "x"s from A is impossible to detect: it would need two unlikely transitions (A to C and C to A), and "x" is more likely in A anyway. This illustrates the main limitation of decoding: when the state distributions overlap, short visits to a state cannot be recovered. The local decoding probabilities in the table give the same sequence here, but they also show the uncertainty: $P(A \mid \mathbf{x})$ is only about 0.75 for the first observations, and at time 8 the probabilities for B and C are close.

## Question 3: Probability of three observations from a Poisson HMM

The two-state Poisson HMM has $\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 0.1 & 0.9 \\ 0.4 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (1, 3)$. Since the HMM is stationary, $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ is the stationary distribution, which solves $\boldsymbol{\delta}\Gamma = \boldsymbol{\delta}$: $\boldsymbol{\delta} = (4/13, 9/13)$.

**a) Summing over all** $2^3 = 8$ state sequences:

$$
P(X_1 = 0, X_2 = 2, X_3 = 1) = \sum_{c_1, c_2, c_3} \delta_{c_1}\gamma_{c_1c_2}\gamma_{c_2c_3} \, p_{c_1}(0)\,p_{c_2}(2)\,p_{c_3}(1).
$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q3
#| tbl-cap: "All eight state sequences for the observations (0, 2, 1): the probability of the state sequence, the probability of the observations given the sequence, and their product."

Gamma_q3 = matrix(c(0.1, 0.9, 0.4, 0.6), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
lambda_q3 = c(1, 3)
delta_q3 = stat_dist(Gamma_q3)
x_q3 = c(0, 2, 1)

paths = expand.grid(C1 = 1:2, C2 = 1:2, C3 = 1:2) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(`P(states)` = delta_q3[C1] * Gamma_q3[cbind(C1, C2)] * Gamma_q3[cbind(C2, C3)],
         `P(x | states)` = dpois(x_q3[1], lambda_q3[C1]) * dpois(x_q3[2], lambda_q3[C2]) *
                           dpois(x_q3[3], lambda_q3[C3]),
         Product = `P(states)` * `P(x | states)`) |>
  arrange(C1, C2, C3)

kable(paths, digits = 6)
```

**b) The matrix formula:**

```{r}
P_q3 = function(x) diag(dpois(x, lambda_q3))

c(delta = delta_q3,
  sum_over_paths = sum(paths$Product),
  matrix_formula = as.numeric(delta_q3 %*% P_q3(0) %*% Gamma_q3 %*% P_q3(2) %*%
                                Gamma_q3 %*% P_q3(1) %*% rep(1, 2)))
```

Both methods give $P(X_1 = 0, X_2 = 2, X_3 = 1) = `r round(sum(paths[["Product"]]), 6)`$. The matrix formula does the same sum, but by summing over the state at each time point as it goes, instead of listing every sequence. With $m$ states and $T$ observations, listing the sequences takes $m^T$ terms (each a product of about $2T$ factors), while the matrix product (the forward algorithm) takes about $Tm^2$ operations. @tbl-q3 also shows that the sequence (1, 2, 1) contributes most: a 0 is most likely from state 1 ($\lambda = 1$), a 2 is more likely from state 2 ($\lambda = 3$), and a 1 is again more likely from state 1. The transitions $1 \to 2$ (0.9) and $2 \to 1$ (0.4) are also reasonably likely.

## Question 4: The independent mixture as a special case

If the Markov chain degenerates to a sequence of independent random variables, then $P(C_t = j \mid C_{t-1} = i) = P(C_t = j) = \delta_j$ for every $i$. So every row of $\Gamma$ equals $\boldsymbol{\delta}$, i.e. $\Gamma = \mathbf{1}'\boldsymbol{\delta}$, and $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ is also the initial distribution. Then for any $x$,

$$
\mathbf{P}(x_{t-1})\Gamma = \mathbf{P}(x_{t-1})\mathbf{1}'\boldsymbol{\delta},
$$

and therefore every factor can be split off:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_T &= \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_2)\Gamma\cdots\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_T)\mathbf{1}' \\
&= \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_1)\mathbf{1}'\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_2)\mathbf{1}'\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\cdots\mathbf{1}'\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_T)\mathbf{1}' \\
&= \prod_{t=1}^{T}\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_t)\mathbf{1}' = \prod_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_i\,p_i(x_t;\theta_i),
\end{aligned}
$$

because each $\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_t)\mathbf{1}' = \sum_i \delta_i p_i(x_t)$ is a scalar. This is the likelihood of an independent mixture model with mixing weights $\delta_1, \dots, \delta_m$, as required.

```{r}
# Numerical check with Poisson example from Question 3 (Gamma with identical rows):
Gamma_ind = rbind(delta_q3, delta_q3)
c(hmm = hmm_loglik(sapply(lambda_q3, function(l) dpois(x_q3, l)), delta_q3, Gamma_ind),
  mixture = sum(log(sapply(x_q3, function(x) sum(delta_q3 * dpois(x, lambda_q3))))))
```

My forward algorithm gives exactly the mixture log-likelihood when the rows of $\Gamma$ are identical.

## Question 5: Building an HMM by inspection

### The first string

```{r}
#| label: q5-string1

string1 = paste0("AABBBACABBBACAAAAAAAAABBBACAAAAABACAAAAAABBBBAC",
                 "AAAAAAAAAAAABACABACAABBACAAABBBBACAAABACAAAABAC",
                 "AABACAAABBACAAAABBBBACABBACAAAAAABACABACAAABACA",
                 "ABBBACAAAABACABBACA")
symbols1 = strsplit(string1, "")[[1]]
table(symbols1)

# Split string at every C and describe each segment:
segments = strsplit(string1, "C")[[1]]
head(segments)

# Check every complete segment has form A...A B...B A:
complete = segments[-length(segments)]
all(grepl("^A*B+A$", complete))

run_A = nchar(sub("B+A$", "", complete))     # length of run of A's
run_B = nchar(gsub("[^B]", "", complete))    # length of run of B's

kable(tibble(Run = c("A (before the B's)", "B"),
             Segments = length(complete),
             `Total symbols` = c(sum(run_A), sum(run_B)),
             `Mean run length` = c(mean(run_A), mean(run_B)),
             `Estimated stay probability` = c((sum(run_A) - length(run_A)) / sum(run_A),
                                              (sum(run_B) - length(run_B)) / sum(run_B))),
      digits = 3)
```

The string has a very regular structure. It always cycles through

$$
\underbrace{A\cdots A}_{\text{run of A's}}\ \underbrace{B\cdots B}_{\text{run of B's}}\ A\ C,
$$

followed by the next run of A's (the last segment, a single "A", is the start of a new cycle). C is always preceded and followed by an A, and a run of B's is always followed by exactly one A and then a C. So an "A" behaves differently depending on where it is: after a C, an A can be followed by more A's or by a B, but after a B, an A is always followed by a C. One state for A is therefore not enough, and I propose a **four-state HMM** (@tbl-string1):

| State         | Emits             | Transitions                                              |
|----------------|----------------|-----------------------------------------|
| 1: "A-run"    | A (probability 1) | stay in 1 with probability $p_A$, move to 2 with $1-p_A$ |
| 2: "B-run"    | B (probability 1) | stay in 2 with probability $p_B$, move to 3 with $1-p_B$ |
| 3: "single A" | A (probability 1) | move to 4 with probability 1                             |
| 4: "C"        | C (probability 1) | move to 1 with probability 1                             |

: Proposed HMM for the first string. {#tbl-string1}

$$
\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} p_A & 1-p_A & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & p_B & 1-p_B & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \ \ (\text{columns: A, B, C}), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\delta} = (1, 0, 0, 0).
$$

The string starts with a run of A's, so the initial state is 1. The time spent in a state with stay probability $p$ is geometric with mean $1/(1-p)$, so $p$ can be estimated from the run lengths: $\hat{p} = (\text{total symbols} - \text{number of runs})/\text{total symbols}$. This gives $\hat{p}_A = `r round((sum(run_A) - length(run_A)) / sum(run_A), 2)`$ and $\hat{p}_B = `r round((sum(run_B) - length(run_B)) / sum(run_B), 2)`$ (mean runs of `r round(mean(run_A), 1)` A's and `r round(mean(run_B), 1)` B's). In this model the emissions are deterministic, so the "hidden" part is only that two states emit A. It is still an HMM, because A from state 1 and A from state 3 cannot be told apart without the context.

```{r}
# Simulate string from proposed model to check it looks like the data:
p_A = (sum(run_A) - length(run_A)) / sum(run_A)
p_B = (sum(run_B) - length(run_B)) / sum(run_B)
Gamma_s1 = matrix(c(p_A, 1 - p_A, 0, 0,
                    0,   p_B, 1 - p_B, 0,
                    0,   0,   0,   1,
                    1,   0,   0,   0), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
emit_s1 = c("A", "B", "A", "C")

state = 1
sim_string = character(160)
for (t in 1:160) {
  sim_string[t] = emit_s1[state]
  state = sample(1:4, 1, prob = Gamma_s1[state, ])
}
paste(sim_string, collapse = "")
```

The simulated string has the same structure as the observed one.

### The second string

```{r}
#| label: q5-string2

string2 = "CEFBAFCEFBAFBAFCEFCADCAFBEFCEFBEFBEFCAFCEDCAFBEDCADBAFCAFCEF"
triplets = substring(string2, seq(1, 58, by = 3), seq(3, 60, by = 3))
triplets

pos = tibble(first = substr(triplets, 1, 1),
             second = substr(triplets, 2, 2),
             third = substr(triplets, 3, 3))

table(pos$first)
table(pos$second)
table(pos$third)

# Check if second symbol is related to first:
table(pos$first, pos$second)
```

The 60 symbols split into 20 triplets, and each position of a triplet uses its own pair of symbols: the first symbol is always B or C, the second always A or E, and the third always D or F. This is a **three-state HMM with a deterministic cycle**:

$$
\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\delta} = (1, 0, 0),
$$

with emission probabilities estimated from the counts (@tbl-string2):

| State | A                                     | B                                    | C                                    | D                                    | E                                     | F                                    |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| 1     | 0                                     | `r round(mean(pos$first == "B"), 2)` | `r round(mean(pos$first == "C"), 2)` | 0                                    | 0                                     | 0                                    |
| 2     | `r round(mean(pos$second == "A"), 2)` | 0                                    | 0                                    | 0                                    | `r round(mean(pos$second == "E"), 2)` | 0                                    |
| 3     | 0                                     | 0                                    | 0                                    | `r round(mean(pos$third == "D"), 2)` | 0                                     | `r round(mean(pos$third == "F"), 2)` |

: Emission probabilities for the second string. {#tbl-string2}

The string starts with C, which only state 1 emits, so $\boldsymbol{\delta} = (1, 0, 0)$. The cross-table of the first and second symbols shows that B and C are each followed by A and E about equally often, so it is reasonable to treat the emissions as independent given the state, which is what an HMM assumes. With only 20 triplets the emission probabilities are rough estimates.

## Question 6: The occasionally dishonest casino

This is the classic example from Durbin et al. (1998). A fair die (state 1) and a loaded die that rolls a six half of the time (state 2) are switched according to $\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.05 \\ 0.10 & 0.90 \end{pmatrix}$.

```{r}
#| label: q6

Gamma_cas = matrix(c(0.95, 0.05, 0.10, 0.90), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
emit_cas = rbind(fair   = rep(1/6, 6),
                 loaded = c(rep(1/10, 5), 5/10))
delta_cas = stat_dist(Gamma_cas)

# Simulate 300 rolls:
n_cas = 300
die = numeric(n_cas)
roll = numeric(n_cas)
for (t in 1:n_cas) {
  die[t] = if (t == 1) sample(1:2, 1, prob = delta_cas) else sample(1:2, 1, prob = Gamma_cas[die[t - 1], ])
  roll[t] = sample(1:6, 1, prob = emit_cas[die[t], ])
}

# Decode with the true parameters:
dens_cas = t(emit_cas[, roll])
vit_cas = hmm_viterbi(dens_cas, delta_cas, Gamma_cas)$states
local_cas = hmm_local(dens_cas, delta_cas, Gamma_cas)

c(stationary_P_loaded = delta_cas[2],
  share_loaded = mean(die == 2),
  six_rate_fair = mean(roll[die == 1] == 6),
  six_rate_loaded = mean(roll[die == 2] == 6),
  viterbi_accuracy = mean(vit_cas == die),
  local_accuracy = mean(apply(local_cas, 1, which.max) == die))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-casino
#| fig-cap: "Three hundred simulated rolls from the occasionally dishonest casino. Top: the rolls, with the periods when the loaded die was used shaded. Bottom: the posterior probability that the loaded die is used (local decoding), with the Viterbi path in pink."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

cas_df = tibble(t = 1:n_cas, roll = roll, loaded = die == 2,
                p_loaded = local_cas[, 2], viterbi = vit_cas - 1)

shade = cas_df |>
  filter(loaded) |>
  transmute(xmin = t - 0.5, xmax = t + 0.5)

p_rolls = ggplot(data = cas_df, mapping = aes(x = t, y = roll)) +
  geom_rect(data = shade, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_point(col = col_main, size = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
  labs(title = "Rolls (grey = loaded die).", x = NULL, y = "Roll")+
  theme_minimal()

p_decode = ggplot(data = cas_df, mapping = aes(x = t)) +
  geom_rect(data = shade, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line(aes(y = p_loaded), col = col_main) +
  geom_step(aes(y = viterbi), col = col_accent) +
  labs(title = "Decoded state.", x = "Roll", y = "P(loaded | rolls)")+
  theme_minimal()

p_rolls / p_decode
```

The chain spends about a third of the time with the loaded die ($\delta_2 = 1/3$), and in the simulation sixes are much more frequent when the loaded die is used. The Viterbi path recovers the die correctly for `r round(100 * mean(vit_cas == die))`% of the rolls (@fig-casino). Decoding works because the loaded die is used for runs of about 10 rolls ($1/(1-0.9)$), so a cluster of sixes is good evidence of a switch. Short visits to the loaded die are usually missed, and the switches are detected a few rolls late, because a single six is also quite likely from the fair die.

## Question 7: A two-state Bernoulli HMM

With $P(X_t = x \mid C_t = 1) = 0.5$ for $x = 0, 1$ and $P(X_t = 1 \mid C_t = 2) = 1$,

$$
\mathbf{P}(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{P}(1) = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: q7

Gamma_q7 = matrix(c(0.5, 0.5, 0.25, 0.75), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
delta_q7 = c(1, 2) / 3
p1_q7 = c(0.5, 1)                         # P(X = 1 | C = i)

P_q7 = function(x) diag(if (x == 1) p1_q7 else 1 - p1_q7)

# Likelihood with the matrix product:
bern_hmm_lik = function(x, delta, Gamma) {
  L = delta %*% P_q7(x[1])
  for (t in seq_along(x)[-1]) L = L %*% Gamma %*% P_q7(x[t])
  as.numeric(L %*% rep(1, length(delta)))
}

c(check_stationary = stat_dist(Gamma_q7),
  P_X_equals_0 = as.numeric(delta_q7 %*% P_q7(0) %*% rep(1, 2)),
  P_X_equals_1 = as.numeric(delta_q7 %*% P_q7(1) %*% rep(1, 2)),
  L_111 = bern_hmm_lik(c(1, 1, 1), delta_q7, Gamma_q7),
  `29/48` = 29 / 48,
  L_111_forward = exp(hmm_loglik(t(sapply(c(1, 1, 1), function(x) diag(P_q7(x)))), delta_q7, Gamma_q7)))
```

The stationary distribution is $\boldsymbol{\delta} = \frac{1}{3}(1, 2)$, so marginally $P(X_t = 0) = \frac{1}{3}(0.5) = 1/6$ and $P(X_t = 1) = 5/6$. The likelihood of three 1's is $\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(1)\mathbf{1}' = 29/48 \approx 0.604$, which both my matrix-product function and my forward algorithm reproduce. This is larger than $(5/6)^3 \approx 0.579$, the value if the observations were independent, because a 1 makes state 2 more likely, and state 2 is persistent and always emits 1.
